QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE.-CHARGES AGAINST THE ADMINISTRATION OF THE GOVERNMENT SHIPYARD AT SOREL AND THE MEMBER FOR RICHELIEU.
speechtext:
(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege to present the motion of which notice has been given two days ago to the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur) and to the hon. member for Richelieu.
Neither the hon. minister nor the hon. member will be surprised at my mov". because they already know since a long time the facts which I will communicate to the House.
I would have been particularly grateful to them if, during the long months that have elapsed since, they had undertaken, themselves, as is was proper, to avenge the honour of the minister and the reputation of the member. But they
have done nothing. They have kept about the whole thing a very long silence which I would dare to qualify as incriminating. I for one cannot allow this silence to last longer without feeling myself as conniving, or at least as.failing seriously in my duty as a member of this House.
I shall read in English the declaration and the motion, and with your permission, Mr. Speaker, I shall read in French, in their original form, the affidavits which have been given me. I have 'added also, since the notice I have given, the years 1908 and 1909 to the year 1910, because new affidavits have come to me.
I,	Pierre Edouard Blondin, a member of Parliament for the electoral district of Champlain, in the province of Quebec, Dominion of Canada, declare that I am credibly informed, and I believe that I can establish by satisfactory evidence:
10. That in the course of the years 1908, 1909 and 1910, irregularities, abuses, frauds, malversations and robberies have been committed in the shops and stores of the government of Canada at St. Joseph of Sorel and in the city of Sorel, in the electoral district of Richelieu;
20. That barrels aud tins of paint and other goods of this nature have been illegally and fraudulently taken and carried away from the said stores and shops and transported to the house of Mr. Adelard Lanctot then and now a member of the House of Commons of Canada, for the electoral district of _ Richelieu, which house was then being built on George street, at Sorel above mentioned, and ready to be painted;
30. That with these goods and paint, paint-works, decoration and varnish works, have been done by the employees of the government of Canada under the supervision of the painters' foreman employed by said government at the said jilace, at the government's expense and during the hours supposed to be devoted to the government and for which said employees were paid by the government, these men registering each day as if they had really worked for the government, and this during weeks and months; the materials and time, thus furnished, are valued at about one thousand or twelve hundred dollars;
40. That said goods were so fraudulently appropriated to, and said work so fraudulently done at the expense of the government of Canada for the benefit of the said Adelard Lanctot then and now a member of the House as aforesaid with his knowledge, assent and approval, the said Adelard Lancjtot abusively and fraudulently profiting at the public expense and to the public detriment by bis position of member of the House;
I found the belief I have just expressed upon affidavits which I desire to read and produce in support of the motion I am about to make:

I, the undersigned, Alfred Douaire, painter, of the city of Sorel, 51 years of age, solemnly declare:

That I have been in the employment of the federal government at its shipyards situated at Saint-Joseph de Sorel, from January, 1906, inclusively to the 5bh of November, i910, as painter under the orders of J. Bte. Page, foreman of the painters department at the said shipyards, during the last two years;-that during these two said years, principally during the last year, and especially in July, August and September, 1910, I have been requested by the said J. Bte. Page to go to Sorel, at the house of Mr. Adelard Lanctot, M.P., then being built on George street, in order to paint, cement, polish and varnish, &c., &c., the said house and that, as it was well understood, after having registered at the shipyard as present and working on behalf of the government, and my departure each morn-in!.' was to be from the said shipyard.
That, as a matter of fact, I regularly registered and punched as previously mentioned, and that in conformity with my orders I left the shipyard each working day and went, as above stated, during the months of July, August and September, 1910, to the said Lanc tot house, where I have worked at the painting, varnishing and staining of the said Lanctot house.
That this work was also done in part by *Messrs. Theodore Emond, Edmond Brault, Adelard Letendre, Alberique Letendre, Omer Page, Arthur Trempe, Louis Paul, Adelard A lie, all painters, employed at the time by the said government, and on the working hours due to the government and each of them having punched at the same time as myself as aforesaid.
That during the time that work was going on, the said J. Bte. Page and Adelard Lanctot, M.P., were visiting the job from time to time, looking at the progress of the work, Page giving orders for having some paint brought from the shipyard and also fo.r the execution of the work, and that, many times to the knowledge and cognizance, and in the presence of the said Adelard Lanctot,-this gentleman knowing also where the paint came from and that the work was being done by employees of the government whom . he was seeing often and often at work.
That_ the said Adelard Lanctot never spoke of paying these painters, and in fact was not paying them, but they were regularly paid their salaries by the government at each pay day, as if they had worked for the department.
That the above mentioned persons who have worked with me at this painting have given to that work, some four weeks, and others from four to ten weeks.
I positively declarethat Mr. Adelard Lanctot knew at the time that the paint and other goods which were used in the painting of his house, were coming from the said shipyard of the government; 2. that this work was done by the then regular employees of the government who were paid, for the time they were doing that work, by the government itself, and that for that purpose the time of each employee was punched as employee of the government.
On the seventh day of December, 1910, at 10 p.m., Mr. Alfred Lavallee, lumber merchant, of Sorel, came to my house at Sorel, asking Mr. BLONDIN.
me to go immediately to the house of Mr. Adelard Lanctot, at Sorel, who desired to see me without fault; I went immediately and found Mr. Lanctot who was waiting for me and who, after the ordinary salutations, showed me and read me the solemn declaration which I had given during the said month of December to the same purpose as the present one, and spoke to me the following words:-* Is it you, Mr. Donaire, who gave this affidavit?' I answered: 'Yes.' He added: ' You have signed it?' I answered 'Yes.' He asked me if I would see Albert Thibaudeau and try to lay my hand upon certains papers relating to this affair, which he did not like to see circulating. I answered that it was not easy to get hold of these documents, principally the affidavit dated at Sorel. the 30th of November,, 1910. Mr. Lanctot added: ' I will look to that myself, and I will try to get hold of them. Mr. Lanctot wanted me to change my course of action, lie offered me a position under the government, which I refused. He told me that if some one was troubled about that affair, principally Mr. J. Bte. Page, I would be treated the same way he would be. I answered that I was not afraid. Before leaving, I told him that the affidavit which lie had in his hands, and which he .got, I did not know from whom, was true and signed by me in perfect knowledge and without any outside influence, as
I gave the present one.
, And I make this solemn statement, believing it conscientiously to be true, and knowing that it lias the same force and effect as if it was made under oath, under the witness law of Canada, and I have signed.
Declared before me, the undersigned, at Sorel, the first of March, 1911.

It is also to my knowledge that in the course of the said work, Cuthbert Champagne, another government employee, and keeper of the punch, had instructions to punch on behalf of the aforesaid painters who did not see to it themselves, in the course of said work, at the said Lanctot house, and that indeed he punched once for me before my arrival, stating: your card is punched as well as the others. Besides, I declare that the said J. Bte. Page, while I was present, addreissel the said Cuthbert Champagne, then close to the punch, and inquired from the .said Champagne, keeper of the punch, whether he was careful to punch regularly on behalf of the men working at the time at Mr. Lanctot's. Mr. Champagne having answered in the affirmative, Mr. Page declared himself satisfied.
I dclare lastly that on the afternoon of the twelfth day, January 6, 1911, I was requested by a friend of Mr. Lanotot to proceed to the letter's office. Accordingly, I wTent and found there Mr. Lanctot, Mr. Joseph Proulx, of Sorel, and Mr. Napoleon Proulx, of St. Vic-teire, two of my uncles, and here is what happened:	'Mir. Adelard Lanctot, M.P., inquired : ' Mr. Proulx, I heard that you weve anxious to get your position; I can have you reinstated provided you 'sign the paper which I have prepared and which I shall read to you. The grist of the paper he then read, was as follows. Hon. minister, I request that you put aside the statement which I signed on November 10, 1910, which you have in your hards. I signed that paper when in a passion and after thinking over it I realized that some things which I had included had no foundation in .fact, and that in the interest of the party as well as in my owTn personal interest such a course would be preferable, and at the same time I beg to be pardoned by you and by the member.' Having ascertained what use the member Lanctot intended to make of this letter, I answered that it was useless to read
any more. ' You should have a better knowledge of the Proulx family; we are not of the kind who sign on Monday and withdraw their signature on Tuesday. I want you to hear in mind .Lauctot that all the affidavits declared and signed by me will remain exactly as on the day I signed them.' Then, Joseph Proulx, ticket agent addressed Lanctot as follows:	' You should not have a
grudge against my nephew, but instead
against those d

whose inspirations you follow.' And the discussion on that subject lasted a couple of hours.
And I make this solemn declaration believing it conscientiously to he true and knowing that it has the same force and effect as if it had been made under oath under the Evidence Act of Canada, and I have signed, HENRI PROULX. Declared before nue, undersigned

I, the undersigned, DieUdonne Peloquin, joiner and contractor of the city of Sorel, do solemnly declare:
1.	That I am 34 years of age and that I have never obtained any contract, or favour, or employment from any of the political parties, and that I am independent of them.
2.	That, to my personal knowledge, during the past five or six months, several men employed in the Dominion government shipyards situated at St. Joseph de Sorel, accused each other of thefts and plunderings of cement, lumber, iron, paint, and especially of time as government employees working for private persons while in the departmental pay; the whole being evidenced by several solemn declarations which have been put in my hands in the course of the last two or three days for the purpose of enlightening me and inducing me to request an investigation.
3.	That in the course of November last and of December instant politicians, officials of the department high and low, accusers and accused, have travelled to Ottawa; one of the storekeepers has been suspended, then reinstated as he threatened to tear asunder the curtain which covered many a deed. Finally calm was restored, and it wa.s rumoured that matters would be set right, the accusers giving way as a rsulit of promises of employment, and the accused being compelled to pay back the value of the goods and time received. Hence an unforeseen appraisal for the purpose of determining the value of certain things which parties interested put down at $292, and which people w'ho have no interest in the matter figure at $800 or $1,000, or even as high as $12,000.
4.	That basing myself on the written and oral statements which have been made and communicated to me, and on rumours deemed trustworthy here, I believe that the government, within the last two years, must have suffered a loss of over fifty thousand dollars, through fraud, embezzlement, etc.
5.	That to my personal knowledge painters

in the employ of the government have painted the inside and outside of the house of our Dominion member of parliament, Mr. Ade-lard Lanctot, who was aware that such work was being carried on by these men, at his house situated on George street, in the city of Sorel; one of the best finished and the best painted in this city, and the painting of which is estimated at prices varying several hundred dollars.
And I make this solemn declaration believing it conscientiously to be true and knowing that it has the same effect and force as if it had been made under oath, under the Evidence Act of Canada.

I, the undersigned, Andronique Senecal, carpenter and joiner, of the city of Sorel, agd 45 years, do solemnly declare:
1. That J am employed at the Dominion government shipyards, situated at St. Joseph do Sorel, at the present time, and have been so employed for the last nine years; that on or about the third of May, nineteen hundred and nine (1909), Oscar Champagne, a man iu the employ of the same government, in the same place, as time-keeper, summoned me from .my work to his office and instructed me tc proceed at once to Sorel, to the house of Adelard Lanctot, then in course of construction on George street, that there I would find Lanctot waiting for me and would he _ told what to do. That accordingly, in compliance with that order from Champagne, I left forthwith, taking with me two ferry tickets, the property of the government, which Champagne handed to me to reach the place of the said Adelard Lanctot at Sorel. On my way I saw Mr. Lanctot at the Hotel Quebec, notwithstanding which I proceeded to his house and. waited for him until the following day. In fact, on the following day, I met Mr. Lanctot at his residence about nine in the morning, and told him that Mr. Champagne had sent me to him for some work that was to be done.
Mr. Lanctot then instructed me to work about the house on his property, repair.;" and resetting the fence which surrounded it; I got to work at once and worked three days iu succession without interruption. I was paid by the government for these three days' work spent at Mr. Lanotot's; I was working under the latter's instructions and he must have seen to have my card punched by obliging bands, for I was paid .in full as usual.
And I make this solemn declaration, believing it to be conscientiously true and knowing that it has the same force and effect a ; if it had been made under oath under the Evidence Act of Canada,
And I have signed.

Mr. Speaker, the charges which I have Just read are sufficient, it seems to me, to allow me dispensing with making any comment. I venture to hope that the government will grant the motion which I have the honour to introduce:
That, under the circumstances, I move that the declarations and matters above set forth bo referred to the Select Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections of this House to inquire fully into the same, with power to send for persons, papers, records and such articles as may be necessary for such investigation, and to examine witnesses upon oath or affirmation, and that the oommitte do re-

pert in full the evidence taken before them and all their proceedings on the reference and result of their inquiries.
I even entertain the hope that the hon. member for Richelieu will join hands with me in requesting that the government grant this inquiry so that he may be in a position to vindicate himself, if possible, and enable us to continue having for him that esteem we have always had heretofore.

I must say that I have no objection whatever to the motion of the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Blondin) asking that the charges preferred against me as a member of this House be referred for investigation to the Committee on Privileges and Elections. I am glad he has brought this matter to the attention of the House, and I court the fullest and most complete investigation of it.
The facts are simply these:	During the
month of June last, I was building a house in Sorel, and when it was ready to be painted I had at the time to leave Sorel very frequently to go to Saranac lake where my wife was lying ill. Not having sufficient time to bring painters to Sorel from any outside place, and knowing that none could be had in the town of Sorel except at the Marine Department shops, and at the Richelieu and Ontario shops, I went to the Marine Department to ask the superintendent Mr. Papineau, to send me a few painters to finish my work. Mr. Papineau being absent, I spoke to Mr. Champagne, the timekeeper, and requested him to send me painters when he could spare them without delaying the work of the department, and I told him to keep an exact, accurate and separate account of the time of these men while working at my house; at the same time, I informed Mr. Page, the foreman, that I had asked for painters from Mr. Champagne, and that Mr. Champagne would keep the time of the men while they were working at my place. I told Mr. Page to get all the necessary materials from Cyrille Labelle & Co., with whom I was dealing, and where I had an account current for supplies used in my building. I also explained to Mr. Page that I was leaving for Saranac, lake to join my wife, and that I relied upon him to see that the men did their work properly, requesting him at the same time to render me the accounts as the work was proceeding that I might pay them, to avoid any misunderstanding in the matter. Men were sent at various times between the months of June and November to do this work, and during that period, when I asked at different times that the account he rendered to me, I was told that it would be more simple and would involve less work to render the account when the work was finished. The Mr. BLONDIN.
men did the work, and when the same was finished, the bill was rendered to me by Mr. Champagne for the department and I immediately paid it in full upon its production.
Some of the paint, varnish and other materials used were obtained from the shops of the Department of Marine and Fisheries. An accurate account of such materials was kept, and goods of the same quality and to the same quantity were purchased to replace the same, and the account for the goods so purchased together with costs of carriage to Sorel was paid by me and goods were returned to the department immediately.

PRIVILEGE-TYPHOID	EPIDEMIC IN

Mr. Speaker, I Tise to a question of privilege. On Thursday last, I made a few remarks in which I referred to the water service of the city of Ottawa. I also referred to some statistics of infantile mortality in Ottawa. In Saturday's Ottawa ' Citizen,' there was an editorial commenting upon what I said. The editorial reads in part as follows:

The attack of Dr. Black, M.P., upon Ottawa water conditions in the House of Commons has, unfortunately, attracted much outside attention. The term unfortunate is used because it is a matter of regret that a statement destined to attain such publicity should have contained assertions which are, in many cases, not borne out by facts.
Dr. Black made the surprising claim that Ottawa water has been polluted for several years past and that the presence of typhoid bacilli had been demonstrated therein. As a matter of fact such a statement is at variance with the records. The tests of city water, conducted perhaps irregularly, have never shown any trace of typhoid bacilli, and to this more probably than anything else was due the irregularity of the tests. Had these shown typhoid germs at any time the medical health officer certainly would have made the fact known. Typhoid has yet to be demonstrated in Ottawa water. _
Dr. Black also asserts that it is known where the present outbreak has originated. If so, it is not a matter of common knowledge and Dr. Black- is not using the city fairly by withholding such information, particularly at this time. We may be getting poisoned, as Dr. Black intimates, but we can still conscientiously plead that we _ don't know how any more than at the beginning of the present outbreak.
It might also be interesting if Dr. Black were to give us the source or authority for the statement that 626 infants out of 2,100 born in the year ending October 31, 1910, in this city, died in infancy. The figures seem alarmingly large, but if correct, the city owes

the honourable member an expression of thanks for calling attention to such a condition.
I need not read the rest of this article. In referring to what the editor says, let me take the last statement first. The ' Citizen ' wants to know where I got my figures. It affords me pleasure, and no little comfort to inform the ' Citizen ' that I got these figures from the ' Citizen.' When I gave these figures, I was quoting from the ' Citizen ' of December 29, 1910. I will read the paragraph to show that I made no mistake:
The city hall figures show that, excluding entirely 143 deaths in two children's homes-
I want you to note that the paragraph divides the death rate into two different lots, giving the percentage of one and not of the other, while I added them and gave the percentage of the whole.
-483 deaths of children under one year took place in the year ending October 31 last. The last birth rate published for 1908 gave 25-5 births per 1,000 in Ottawa. Taking this as a rough basis, we find that there would have been last year 2,100 births, of whom 483, or 230 in 1,000 died. I am limiting myself to it, and if I get beyond that please correct me. This paper said that I said that typhoid bacillus was in the water. I did unfortunately say that, but it was a slip of the tongue, and not due to a lack of knowledge of the matter. My mind was so full of typhoid at the time that I said ' typhoid bacillus ' instead of ' colon bacillus '. The merest tyro in water analysis knows that the typhoid bacillus is the most difficult bacillus to find in water. Sometimes, with great difficulty, it is found in milk, but it has been shown over and over again that colon bacilli are present in the Ottawa water and have been. Colon bacilli and typhoid bacilli are room mates living side by side in the same space in the human system. Their lives run parallel in the human body and when present in the Ottawa river their lives run parallel and the tendency is to die. You find colon bacilli quite readily by analysis, but the typhoid bacillus is very, very difficult to find, so difficult that whenever colon bacilli are found it is assumed, as a matter of course, that their running mate, the typhoid bacillus is there also. When colon bacilli are found it follows as a natural assumption that typhoid will result. Colon bacilli have been found in the water year after vear, and this proves that the trouble exists in the water. To contradict this statement, I want to say this: There are four wavs in which typhoid is carried-water, milk, flies, contact. Let us take them one by one.

_ Mr. BLAIN. I would like to ask a question of the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence (Sir Frederick Borden). Perhaps I can do it better by reading the following *despatch:
ABUSE OF PATRONAGE Claimed in Connection With the Coronation Contingent.
Ottawa, Feb. 20.-(Special.)-Members of parliament are considerably aroused over Mr. BLACK.
what is claimed to be a shameful abuse of patronage in connection with the selection of the officers for the Canadian coronation contingent. About thirty officers are to be chosen, and in Toronto and other places the local patronage committees are dealing with the matter and passing their recommendations on to the Minister of Militia.
lit is stated: 'Instead of a fine body of men chosen to represent Canada oh their merits being sent to the coronation, faithful friends of the government will be among the elect.' Officers whose service and seniority entitle them to place are being ignored.
I do not know anything of the correctness of this report, but I thought I would give the minister an opportunity to deny it here.
Who sends the telegram?
It is a newspaper despatch; I will hand it over to my hon. friend.
From what newspaper?
It is a despatch from Ottawa to Toronto ' World.'

Oh, from Ottawa! Mr. Speaker, a question was asked in the House by two or three hon. members as to the principle upon which the selection would be made for the coronation contingent. I answered the question very fully. As far as the selection of the men who will compose the contingent is concerned, they will be selected absolutely and entirely by the commanding officers of their respective corps from which the men are taken. There will be a proper percentage selected from every corps, or every regiment in the whole Dominion. No selection will be made from Ottawa; the headquarters' staff or the minister will have absolutely nothing to do with the selection. That is, as far as the non-commissioned officers and men are concerned. In so far as the officers are concerned, the principle upon which they are being selected is also laid down in the answer which I gave. No officers who have already attended a similar function, for instance, the coronation of 1902 and the jubilee of 1897, will be allowed to attend the coronation. Officers who have had war service and medals will be preferred. No officer will be allowed to serve in a rank junior to that in which he is serving in the militia. That is to say, no officer will be allowed to attend the coronation in a rank junior to his own if he is not within the age limit of that junior rank, the reason being that there are officers who are very keen to attend this function, who, being majors, we will say, or even lieutenant-colonels, would be quite willing to attend in a junior rank for the sake of going. We have made it a regulation that, say a major, will not be allowed to attend in any

rank junior to the rank of major unless he is within the age limit. For instance, it might be convenient to take a major as captain-the next rank below-but he would not be allowed to serve as captain unless he is within the age limit of a captain.
If a subordinate is willing to go as a sergeant, or even as a private, what would be the rule?

I do not think that would be right. I do not think we should allow any commissioned officer to serve as a non-commissioned officer, or as a private; that is the position I have taken. Now, as-regards this telegram, I can only say it is a tissue of falsehoods from beginning to end; perhaps that is the best way to describe it. Whether Liberal com-mitteees, or Conservative committees for that matter, may have met and passed resolutions; I do not know for a fact, although I do not think it is a fact. But if it were a fact I wish to say at once, Mr. Speaker, it would have no influence whatever on me. Regiments have	met-one
regiment of the city of Ottawa has indicated that they wish a certain officer to be taken if any officer is to go from that regiment. The officers of the 5th Royal Highlanders of Montreal have also met and selected an officer, and I would think, Mr. Speaker, that assuming the officer so selected came within the regulations, I should be under an' obligation to accept that officer if any officer is to be taken from those regiments. I wish to say, if I may add a word, that the difficulty of the situation is very considerable. There are to be chosen 48 officers altogether, eight or ten of whom will necessarily be of the permanent force, so that there will be some thirty-eight officers to be chosen from the active militia of Canada, which comprises between 3,500 and 4,000 officers. There are something like 100 or 120 different military corps, regiments, squadrons, or units in the militia, so that on an average there will be one officer from every 3 or 4 corps.
Will there be representatives taken from each province?
Yes.
Is it the purpose to send a detachment of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police?

There will be, as there was in 1902, a certain percentage of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police in the contingent, but that is being attended to by the department in charge. It is. perhaps, convenient for me to say now that the first thing we have to do is to carefully consider the relative number of
the different branches of the service, cavalry, artillery, infantry and some of the minor services, and if possible, and so far as possible, to properly divide the contingent up according to strength among these different branches of the service. Then we have to consider provinces; every province in the Dominion must be represented by both officers and men. Some of the provinces may not be entitled to more than one officer, but every province will receive its fair share of representation among the commissioned officers, the non-commissioned officers and men. It is a difficult task. I am getting the best help I can from headquarters here and from other parts of the militia throughout the country to enable me to solve the difficulty fairly and with due regard to all interests, and also to enable Canada to present, on such a memorable occasion, a contingent which in every respect will be worthy the country it represents.
Have the commandants been selected? It is reported in the newspapers that Col. Woods and others have been selected?

The commandant is to be Col. McLean, a member of this House. No other selections have been absolutely determined. At an early date, perhaps when the militia estimates come up, I hope to be able to submit to the House at least a progress estimate as to what has been done.

If one of the officers of the contingent should be serving in a rank junior to that which he holds in the militia, what uniform will he wear in the. contingent, that of his actual rank or that of the rank he is serving in?

That is a Question of detail which I would not like to answer, but as I understand it-I think it was done in 1902-an order in council will be passed appointing all the officers to this special service, sp that I should think -although I speak now under correction- that the officer should wear the uniform of the rank in which he serves in the contingent.
What will be the strength of the contingent?.
I think we are invited to send a contingent about 700 strong, which would, of course, include officers.
Perhaps the Prime Minister would tell us now how many officers and men of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police will be sent on the contingent?

MUTILATION OF MAILS. DELAYS IN DEAD LETTER BRANCH.
speechtext:
1.	Has the government ever tried using elastic bands instead of string to hold bundle! of letters together, in outside offices? If so. with what success, and if not, why not? '
2.	Has the government recently investigated the carriage of mail matter between Kingston and Ottawa? If so, what irregularities have been found as to delays in transmission of mail, irregular delivery at Ottawa, and careless handling of His Majesty's mail?
3.	If this investigation has not been made, why not, and will the government institute-ail immediate investigation into these complaints?
4.	Has the government inquired into the cause of delay in returning letters sent to the dead letter office, and have instructions been given to return them more promptly to the owner?
5.	Does the government make frequent tests of the tensile strength of the paper out of which the mutilated envelopes, sent in along with complaints, are made?
6.	Does the government make inquiry into all the complaints received regarding mutilated envelopes? If so, what action is taken to improve the system?

subtopic: MUTILATION OF MAILS. DELAYS IN DEAD LETTER BRANCH.
speechtext:
_
1. No. It has never seemed a necessity to do so, as tying them with twine has been an absolute success, and is in use in every postal country in the world. Elastic bands after being once or twice used could not be relied upon, owing to the loss of elasticity, and wonld be of no use in keeping letters together. The use of elastic bands would, as compared with the cotton twine now specially manufactured for the purpose, immensely enhance the cost of the transmission of the mails, since, in addition to the perishability of the bands, a large variety, as regards size, thickness and width, would be required to be held in stock at every post office. Moreover, no .complaint has been made throughout the whole of Canada, except by the one business firm.
2	and 3. The department has no reason to believe that other than the schedule time is required for the transmission of mail matter between Kingston and Ottawa. A search of the departmental records covering a period of one year, however, reveals the fact that three complaints were received from the E. B. Eddy Company, Limited, Hull, respecting delay in tho transmission of their correspondence between Kingston and Ottawa, and investigation showed that in only two of the cases was delay attributable to the postal service. The first case concerned a letter mailed at Kingston on the evening of Friday, the 25th of November, 'and which, it was stated did not reach the addressees until Monday, the 28th of November. In some way or other this letter was missent upon the mail clerk of Ottawa and Calumet, and if Sunday had not intervened, delivery could have been effected one day earlier. The second case referred to a letter mailed at Kingston on the 22nd December, and said not to have been received until the morning of the 24th. Careful inquiry failed to locate responsibility, but it should be pointed out that this alleged delay occurred during the extraordinary pressure oi work consequent upon the Christmas season when-' the mail service was naturally somewhat

subtopic: MUTILATION OF MAILS. DELAYS IN DEAD LETTER BRANCH.
speechtext:
congested with the enormous quantity of matter in course of transmission. The final case related to a letter posted at Kingston at 6 p.m. on the 27th of December, and received by the addressees at 11 a.m. on the 28th. No delay occurred in this instance and the complainants were so advised.
4.	The department has no reason to believe that there is any avoidable delay in the disposal of mail matter received at the dead letter office. The matter was very fully, taken up with the dead letter office less than a month ago, and every possible effort is being made to secure promptness in the return of dead letters.
5.	No. The complaints which have been received in regard to this matter have been exclusively from one source. In this case, the company in question make use of envelopes which are much larger than those usually employed besides being of a more or less brittle character. The consequence is that the damage complained of is probably due as much to the unusual size of the envelope as the character of the paper of which it is made.
6.	Careful investigation is always made into each complaint, and when it is ascertained that the irregularities complained of could be properly charged against the postal service, steps are taken to prevent their recurrence.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. P. BRODEUR (Minister of Marine and Fisheries).
speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, resuming the adjourned debate on the question raised by my hon. friend from Digby (Mr. Jameson), let me say at once that I And no fault with the hon. gentleman for bringing this question before the House. It is certainly an important question, and, under the circumstances, perhaps it is advisable that the matter should be discussed. At the same time, it must be admitted that there is great difficulty in discussing a question which .may be, later on, the subject of further negotiations between Great Britain, on behalf of Canada, and the United States. In such a discussion, views might be expressed that would later on impair the value of negotiations. Consequently, perhaps, it would be better that parliament should refrain as much as possible from discussing such questions. But in such discussions, we should certainly eliminate considerations of party advantage. These international questions are of such importance that the country should be a unit upon them. If it were found that great differences of opinion existed between members of this House upon questions which may be the subject of future negotiations, the freedom of negotiation would be impaired. My hon. friend from Digby and my hon. friend from South Cape Breton (Mr. Maddin) have thought fit to bring into the discussion questions of party politics. I am extremely sorry that such a thing should have been done. I may be in a position, later on, to show that, so far as the government is concerned there is certainly no responsibility, because what has been done has been done in such a way that the government could not be held responsible. If hon. members opposite find it prudent to discuss the question from the party point of view, I would call their attention to the fact that this question of the Bay of Fundy was practically settled by the treaty of 1888, which was negotiated by Sir Charles Tupper, who was at one time leader of the Conservative party and thought fit to exclude the Bay of Fundy from the effect of the treaty.
Now, Sir, my hon. friends opposite have found it advisable to discuss the part taken by the Minister of Justice in connection with the settlement of this question, and of other questions which were settled by the

Hague Tribunal. The hon. the Minister of Justice, along with the British Ambassador, had charge of those negotiations, and I think the success which Canada has achieved before that tribunal shows that very great credit is due to the Minister of Justice for the work he performed in relation thereto. My hon. friend from Digby (Mr. Jameson) and my hon. friend from Cape Breton (Mr. Maddin) have said that the Minister of Justice had gone up and down the country giving lectures upon this question. That is quite true, but it was not done at the initiative of the Minister of Justice himself, but in obedience to invitations from clubs and public bodies to discuss these important national questions. He could not do otherwise, under the circumstances. The facts that he brought out in those addresses have given us more information upon the subject than the community generally was aware of. It is certainly unfair to disparage the work which has been done by the Minister of Justice in connection with the Atlantic fisheries. He devoted many months to that work, not only in the preliminary negotiations, but in the preparation of the case, and in the conduct of the case after the matter was brought before the court at the Hague. 1 think Canada must feel great satisfaction in the fact that we have won on the two most important points submitted to that tribunal, namely, our right to legislate with regard to the treaty coast, and on the question of the bays. When I was in Washington the other day with the Minister of Justice I was able to observe the high opinion which is entertained of him by the representatives of the United States government, and the respect which they have for his legal attainments. His opinion is regarded there, as it is regarded here, as that of a gentleman of the highest legal ability.
Now, Sir, my horn, friend from Cape Breton has thought proper to introduce into the discussion a letter which was written by Mr. Ewart some time ago, and which [was published in the newspapers. Mr. Ewart thought that the construction which was put upon his letter was not an accurate one, and when he knew that this debate had been adjourned, he called upon me and asked me if I would be kind enough to read before the House a letter which he gave me. I will read the letter, because I think it is only fair to the Minister of Justice, and to Mr. Ewart also, that it should go upon the ' Hansard
March 4, 1911.
Dear Mr. Brodeur,-Mr. Maddin is quite mistaken in his belief that my letter 'was evoked, by the fact that the minister had gone up and down this country, speaking before the Canadian Club, before the Bar Association, in this House on December 2, last, and in Halifax during the Christmas holidays, lauding men who were not entitled to his laudation/ etc. It was written, as it Mr. BRODEUR.
says, because of newspaper statements.
I was present at the Canadian Club luncheon, at which Sir Allen spoke and afterwards I thanked him for his kind reference to my work, saying that he had been 'altogether too generous '-meaning that while he had praised my work in connection with the preparation of the case, he had said nothing as to his own, in connection with the diplomatic side of it. So far from objecting to his addresses in Halifax and Toronto, I was aware of his invitations to those places and I ventured to offer him some suggestions that might be useful to him.
And it is not the fact that I am in the least envious of Sir Allen's praise of Sir William Robson's work. I doubt if language could be found which would fully express my own admiration of it, and, I may add, of the work of Sir Robert Finlay. I envy the force and style of those men and not any encomiums which their merits have brought them.
I am, dear Mr. Brodeur,
Yours sincerely,

Now, Sir, in the discussion which has taken place on this question, some disparaging remarks have been made in reference to the part which Mr. Bryce, the British ambassador, has taken in matters in dispute between Canada and the United States. I am extremely sorry that anything should have been said in this House underestimating the value of the co-operation which Mr. Bryce has given to the Canadian government. Not only in this instance, but in all other disputes between the two countries. Mr. Bryce has performed services of very great value to Canada, and not only to Canada, but to the whole British Empire. Mr. Bryce, on account of his famous book on the American commonwealth, in which he described so accurately the institutions of the United States, was in a high degree persona grata to the people of the United States. I may say, however, that when Mr. Bryce was first appointed British ambassador at Washington, there was some feeling among certain classes in Canada that he was likely to be too favourably disposed towards the United States. That feeling, I can assure the House, was not at all shared by the Canadian government, but it is a fact that some feeling of that kind did exist in certain sections of this country. I am glad to say now that this feeling has entirely disappeared, and it is now recognized on all hands that Mr. Bryce has succeeded in bringing about more cordial and friendly relations, not only between the United States and Canada, but between the United States and Great Britain. He has succeeded in maintaining harmoniously both Canadian and British interests, and I may say that he has come to be regarded even as the ambassador of Canada. Some time ago we were glad to see him visit this country, in order to get acquainted with our people and with our institutions, to

inform himself upon public questions, in order that he might be more useful in aiding to settle the issues between the two nations. His visits to Ottawa have been fruitful in that respect, and I hope we will often have an ^opportunity of seeing Ambassador Bryce in this country. The effort to disparage the work which has been done by Mr. Bryce since he has been the British ambassador at Washington is certainly unfair to him when we consider what he has accomplished while he has filled that important position. He was appointed in 1908. I find that since that time no less than ten treaties which concerned Canada and the United States have been negotiated by Mr. Bryce. These treaties are as fol-j lows:	,
1.	General arbitration treaty 4th April, 1908.
2.	Protection of food fishes, 11th April, 1908.
3.	Demarcation of boundaries, 11th April, 1908.
4.	Conveyance of prisoners, 18th May, 1908.
5.	Reciprocity in towing and wrecking, 18th May, 1908.
6.	Boundary waters, 11th May, 1908.
7.	North Atlantic Coast Fisheries Arbitration, 27th January, 1909.
^8^ Passamaquoddy Bay boundary 1st May,
9. Pecuniary claims, 18th August, 1910.
Then there is the agreement which was made the other day when my hon. colleague the Minister of Justice and myself were in Washington, to settle the legality of the legislation which has been passed by the Canadian parliament concerning fisheries on the Atlantic coast. There is also the treaty with reference to pelagic sealing. I do not know whether that treaty has yet been signed, but it is certainly to be signed in a few days, if not already signed. Every hon. member of this House knows that the North Atlantic Coast Fisheries Arbitration Treaty, signed on the 27th January, 1909, made provision for the settlement of a difficulty which has been existing between the two countries for nearly a century. So, Mr. Speaker, within a period of a little more than two years, Mr. Bryce has been able to settle all of these outstanding difficulties, some of which were in existence for many years and, under these circumstances, I "say that it is unfair to disparage the work which has been carried on by him.

If I have the permission of the minister, I would like to say there was no observation made from this side of the House on Friday afternoon last disparaging to the British ambassador. or casting any reflection upon him whatsoever. He will read ' Hansard ' in vain to find any reflection. But, it was pointed out from this side of the House that the Canadian government had the right to confirm any contract which was submitted to
the tribunal, and that this government in ratifying that contract or agreement, or in failing to ratify it, had neglected the rights of the Atlantic fishermen, and we cast the responsibility upon this government and not upon the British ambassador.
