speechtext:
Before we come to the 4th of March; let us see what was done after January 27, 1909. There was a draft signed between Mr. Root and Mr. Bryce, but of course that did not make the treaty effective because under the constitution of the United States a treaty must be assented to by the Senate which, in that respect discharges executive functions. The United States Senate did approve of this treaty but with the condition that the Bay of Fundy should be excluded from the consideration of the tribunal; and on that point I refer to a letter sent by Mr. Bacon to Mr. Bryce, which has not yet been read to the House, but which is to be found in

the appendix to the case of the United States, and which reads:
Department of State, Feb. 21, 1909.
Excellency, I have the honour to inform you that the Senate, by its resolution of the 18th inst. gave its advice and consent to the ratification of the special agreement between the United States and Great Britain, signed on January 27, 1909, for the submission to the Permanent Court of Arbitration at the Hague of questions relating to fisheries on the North Atlantic coast.
In giving this advice and consent to the ratification of the special agreement, and as a part of the act of ratification, the Senate states in the resolution its understanding:
That it is agreed by the United States and Great Britain that question 5 of the series submitted, namely,'from where must be mea-suied the three marine miles of any of the coasts, bays, creeks or harbours referred to i;i said article/ does not include any question as to the Bay of Eundy considered as a whole apart from its bays or creeks or as to innocent passage through the Cut of Can-so and that the respective views or contentions of the United States and Great Britain on either subject shall be in no wise prejudiced by anything in the present arbitration, and that this agreement on the part of the United States will be mentioned in the ratification of the special agreement and will in effect, form part of this special agreement.
In thus formally confirming what I stated to you orally, I have the honour to express the hope that you will in like manner formally confirm the assent of His Majesty's government to this understanding which you heretofore stated to me orally, and that you wilj be prepared at an early day to exchange the notes confirming the special agreement as provided for therein and in the general arbitration convention of June 5, 1908.
I have the honour to be, with the highest consideration, your excellency's most obedient servant,

His Excellency the Rt. Hon. James Bryce,
&c., &c., &c.
This document, I think, answers the question which has been put by the hon. member for North Toronto, as to whether there was some document showing that there was an understanding when the treaty was signed on the 27th of January, 1909. The fact that Mr. Bacon, the Secretary of State, states in his letter to Mr. Bryce that there was an oral understanding before, makes me believe that there was no exchange of documents between them, and I am informed by the Minister of Justice that Mr. Bacon was present during all the negotiations which were carried on between Mr. Bryce and Mr. Root, and he took the place of the Secretary of State on the day of the signing of the treaty, or the next day afterwards. Now, here is the United States Senate saying: We are willing to approve of that treaty, but on the condition that the Bay of Fundy shall be excluded, and later, on the 4th of March, there was an exchange of notes ratifying the treaty 148
made between the British ambassador and the United States Secretary of State. I suppose it is not necessary for me to read them.
My question had reference to the interchange of notes on the 27th of January.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: There was no interchange of notes on the 27th of January.

That is what I asked the minister to permit me to explain, but he would not allow me to do so. That there was an interchange of notes on the 27th of January, 1909, between Mr. Bryce and Mr. Root is evidenced by the fact that Mr. Bryce, in his note of the 4th of March to Mr. Bacon, uses these words:
This understanding (that is, that the Bay of Fund.v should be excluded from the operation of the award) is that which was embodied in note9 exchanged between your predecessor (that was Mr. Root) and myself on the 27th of January, and is that expressed in the above mentioned resolution of the Senate of the United States.
The note of the 27th of January is the one we are looking for.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: The Minister of Justice tells me that he did not know anything about these notes, but there seems to be some difference between the two letters. In the letter of the 21st of February, 1909, which I have just read, from Mr. Bacon to Mr. Bryce, there is reference to an oral understanding. Of course, Mr. Bryce, in his letter of the 4th of March to Mr. Bacon speaks of notes that were exchanged between his predecessor and himself on the 27th of January. Well, that does not alter the situation very much, because whether the objection was made by the Senate itself or by the United States representatives, there is no doubt of this, that the United States would not make a treaty unless the question of. the Bay of Fundy were excluded When we come to discuss the treaty of 1888 we shall find that the United States then took the ground that the question of the Bay of Fund.v should be excluded, and that it should not be treated the same as other bays mentioned in that treaty.

The minister misses the point altogether. The whole point is this, that according to the interchanged note of the 27th of January, 1909, the government of Canada consented to the exclusion of the Bay of Fundy on that date, whereas the Senate of the United States did not resolve that it must be excluded until the 16th day of the following month.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
I do not think that it makes any difference at all, or that I have missed the point of my hon. friend. He charges the government with being respon-

sible for the exclusion of the Bay of Fundy. I say that charge is not well founded, because when we came to negotiate the United States would not consent to include it. During all these negotiations the United States were against including the Bay of Fundy in the question to be adjudicated upon by the tribunal. In this connection I may say that my hon. friend from Cape Breton (Mr. Maddin) stated that the Minister of Justice was in these negotiations representing His Excellency Lord Grey, the Governor General of Canada. I think he must have misunderstood the Minister of Justice, because it was never stated by him that he was representing His Excellency the Governor General.

Sir Edward Grey. I would like to point out to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries that ' Hansard ' is so mutilated and so badly reported that he cannot place very much reliance on it. That is absolutely true of ' Hansard ' for the last four Friday evenings. It is not only my experience, but the experience of other hon. members who had occasion to speak in the House. I am quite sure, speaking from the front bench, my accent and pronunciation are clear and distinct enough to enable me to be properly reported in ' Hansard.' It was not done, and any one who was in the House will recognize a very mutilated report of last Friday evening. It was Sir Edward Grey that I had reference to, and not His Excellency the Governor General.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: It is not a matter of great importance to the discussion whether the Minister of Justice was representing Lord Grey or the Minister of Foreign Affairs. As a matter of fact, in the negotiations carried on at Washington he was acting for the Canadian Government, and later on, when the case was submitted to The Hague Tribunal, and the preparation of the case was entrusted to him, he was not acting as the representative of the Canadian government, but as the agent- of the British government, and in that way was representing, of course, the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Sir Edward Grey.
Who was representing the government of Canada on that occasion?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
The case was submitted, as all international questions are submitted. by the British agent, who is, of course, responsible directly to the Minister of Foreign Affairs, but in this case the Minister of Justice represented Canada also. There were counsel engaged and paid, I think, exclusively by the Canadian government, such as Mr. Ewart and some others. Why was the Bay of Fundy excluded? I have just shown that throughout the negotiations the United States refused to include Mr. BRODEUlt.
it. In the report which I have just quoted of the proceedings of the Senate, I find a letter from Mr. Bacon to Mr. Bryce on the 21st February, 1909, which also shows that the American authorities were insisting on excluding the bay. Why did the United States authorities take this course? Well, the question as to whether the Bay of-Fundy was covered by the treaty of 1818 is a very old one. That treaty provided that the Americans could not fish except at three miles outside the bays. But what was the meaning of the word ' Bay '? Did it cover bays like the Bay of Fundy, the Bale des Chaleurs, Plecentia Bay in Newfoundland, and some others which are more than six or ten miles across? That question caused a good deal of friction, particularly between the province of Nova Scotia and the United States, because the other provinces were not interested with the exception perhaps of New Brunswick. The main contention seemed to have been between the province of Nova Scotia and the United States. We have very often had it said that the blame for the exclusion of the Bay of Fundy should be put on the shoulders of Lord Aberdeen, because of the letter which Lord Aberdeen sent to Mr. Everett on the 10th 'of March, 1845, which letter I shall quote in a few minutes. But it is only fair to the British authorities that I should mention the fact that this step then taken by Lord Aberdeen, who was at the time British Minister of Foreign Affairs, was taken at the suggestion of some members of the cabinet of Nova Scotia and of the governor of that province. Mr. Everett, then" United States minister, contended in his letter of May, 1844, that the Bay of Fundy was not a bay, which came within the treaty prohibition, although he admitted that the smaller bays within the Bay of Fundy did come within it. Of these smaller bays, there are not less than five, which aTe not more than six miles wide each. In his letter of May, 1844, to the British Minister of Foreign Affairs, Mr. Everett said that the American fishermen had the right to go into the Bay of Fundy, but admitted that they could not fish in the other bays inside 'that bay. This letter of Mr. Everett was submitted to the government and the cabinet of Nova Scotia; and as the result of their deliberations. Lord Portland, then governor of Nova Scotia, sent the following letter to the Colonial Office, which will be found interesting under the circumstances. It will be found at page 136 of the Appendix. Here is what he said:
In respect to the expediency of relaxing the strict rule which has hitherto been declared applicable to American vessels found fishing within the limits of the Bay of Fundy, I have found it difficult to arrive at a con-

elusion, because although some members of the Executive Council believe, with myself, that such a concession, provided it led to no other of a like nature, would not be productive of injury to Nova Scotia, and might in fairness be granted, other members of the board, among whom is the Attorney General, entertain a strong opinion to the contrary.
When, however, I perceive that Mr. Everett, in his note of the 25tli May, 1814, addressed to Lord Aberdeen, admits that (in estimating the distance of three miles from the shore within which American fishermen are not permitted to approach) it is 'the intent of the treaty as it is in itself reasonable to have regard to the general line of the coast and to consider its bays, creeks and harbours, that is the indentations so accounted, as included within that line,' which I take to be an acquiescence in the opinion of Messrs. Dodson and Wilde, that the distance within which American fishermen must not approach is three miles from the line drawn from headland to headland, taking the general configuration of the coast; I cannot but conceive that a great portion of what I have contended for (in my despatch No. 75, date May 8, 1841, addressed to Lord John Russell) on the part of the province, is conceded, and it is therefore my unreserved opinion, provided always that this interpretation of Mr. Everett's phraseology be correct, that that which is now asked by the Americans may be granted, without evil consequences, if due care be taken that no further pretentions can hereafter be founded on the concession.
In this letter we have the admission by the governor of Nova Scotia if the Canadian rights in the other bays weTe reserved, he did not see a great deal of harm in the concession asked for, namely, that the Bay of Fundy should be considered as an open sea. It seems to me that the letter which my hon. friend read must be interpreted in the light of the correspondence between Mr. Everett and the governor ol Nova Scotia and the Minister of Colonial Affairs.
When my hon. friend from Digby (Mr. Jameson), says that there is a condition mentioned in the letter of Lord Aberdeen which has not been complied with, I think that he is making a mistake. The cohten-tion made by the American authorities is that the condition gave the exclusive right to the fishermen of Nova Scotia, to fish in the bays which are within the Bay of Fundy, but that the relaxation was made in such terms that American fishermen could fish in the bay itself. In other words, the province of Nova Scotia was willing to accept that the Bay of Fundy should be excluded, or that there should be a relaxation of the conditions though the other bays within the Bay of Fundy were not to be excluded. My hon. friend interprets the condition made in the letter of Lord Aberdeen as being a condition in Tegard to all the bays of Canada. He is mistaken. Let us 148}
read again this part of the letter of Lord Aberdeen:
The undersigned has accordingly much pleasure in announcing to Mr. Everett, the determination which Her Majesty's government have come to relax in favour of the United States fishermen, that right which Great Britain has hitherto exercised, of excluding those fishermen from the British portion of the Bay of Fundy, and they are prepared to direct their colonial authorities to allow, henceforward, the United States fishermen to pursue their avocations in any part of the Bay of Fundy, provided they do not approach, except in the cases specified in the treaty .of 1818, within three miles of the entrance of any bay on the coast of Nova Scotia or New Brunswick.
Now, if we take the last words and compare them with the words we find in the letter of Mr. Everett, we come to the conclusion that, When they speak of the condition excluding them from other bays of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, that means bays within the Bay of Fundy and not outside.

The minister (Mr. Brodeur) differs from the Minister of Justice (Sir Allen Aylesworth) in that respect. At page 671 of the Revised ' Hansard,' the Minister of Justice describes that stipulation in these words:
Upon the stipulation that as to the remainder of the maritime coasts of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Quebec, the claims of United States fishermen should cease.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Precisely. If it had been a question of other bays in Quebec and Newfoundland, it would have been so stated in the letter, but it was not stated, it was simply a reference to bays of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, and in reading the letter of Lord Horton and Mr. Everett, I am led to believe that there is a great deal of force in the contention of the Americans that this applies purely and simply to bays within the Bay of Fundy. I may be mistaken in my interpretatilon of the law, but I think the hon. gentleman will see from the letters I have mentioned that there is a'great deal of force in the contention of the American authorities.
If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Brodeur) says I am mistaken in the view I took the other evening, he says that the Minister of Justice is mistaken.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
I do not say that the Minister of Justice is wrong, but I say there is a great deal of force in the argument made by the American authorities. My hon. friend says that this is a condition which the Americans have not fulfilled. The Americans say:	We have fulfilled our
obligation; we contend that the reservation was of the bays within the Bay of Fundy

and this we have not violated. Mr. Everett in his answer to t'he letter of Lord Aberdeen, maintained the absolute right of the United States fishermen to go into the Bay of Fundy. This letter was dated 25th March, 1845, and the following is an extract from it:
March 25, 1845.
While he desires, however, without reserve, to express his sense of the amicable disposition evinced by Her Majesty's government on this occasion in relaxing in favour of the United States the exercise of what, after deliberate consideration fortified by high legal authority, is deemed an unquestioned right of Her, Majesty's government, the undersigned would be unfaithful to his duty did he omit to remark to Lord Aberdeen that no arguments have at any time been adduced to shake the confidence of the government of the United States in their own construction of the treaty. While they have- even been prepared to admit, that in the letter of one expression of that instrument there is some reason for claiming a right to exclude United States fishermen from the Bay of Fundy (it being difficult to deny to that arm of the sea the name of ' bay' which long geographical usage has assigned to it), they have even strenuously maintained that it is only on their own construction of the entire article that its known design in reference to the regulation of the fisheries admits of being carried into effect.	_
The undersigned does not make this observation for the sake of detracting from the liberality evinced by Her Majesty's government, in relaxing from what they regard as their right; but it would be placing his own government in a false position to accept as mere favour that for which they have so long and strenuously contended as due to them under the constitution.
One point is very clear, and that is that a relaxation was granted under the letter of Lord Aberdeen as to the right of the Americans to fish in the Bay of Fundy. Whether there were or were not conditions attached, and whether these have been fulfilled there may he differences of opinion, but the fact remains that there has been a relaxation, and from 1845 until to-day that relaxation has always been maintained by the British authorities. If the relaxation had been made on the conditions that my hon. friend claims, and if these conditions had not been fulfilled, I suppose we should see some correspondence by which the British authorities would have mentioned the matter to the United States government. But they have not done so, and until today they have always declared that the Americans might fish within the Bay of Fundy.
Now, there is another point that has not been brought out in the discussion which, I think also proves to a very large extent that the- contentions of the Americans that the matter was settled by a treaty, has Mr. BRODEUR.
a great deal of force and should carry weight in any negotiations we may have. I do not wish to be understood as stating that I approve of the contentions made by the Americans in that respect, because 1 do not think it will be advisable to do so in view of the negotiations which may be made later on. But there is a great deal of force, I must admit, in the contention that the Bay of Fundy question has been settled by the Treaty of 1853. The Americans contend, first, that there was a relaxation by the letters of Lord Aberdeen and Mr. Everett, and also that the Treaty of 1853 disposed of this question of the Bay of Fundy. This treaty is called the Russell-fngersoll treaty, and is dated 20th February, 1853. It was made between the United States and Great Britain.
The article of the treaty provided that the pecuniary claims which were made by certain parties should be submitted to a court of arbitration, to be composed of two men, one appointed by the United States government and one appointed lay the British government. The treaty further provided that if these two men could not agree upon any point then a third arbitrator should be appointed. Amongst the claims which were referred to this tribunal under this treaty was the claim made by the United States concerning the seizure of the schooner ' Washington,' which has been mentioned several times in the debate. This vessel was fishing about ten miles from the shore of the Bay of Fundy, and she was seized by the Nova Scotia authorities, I think, as fishing within the territorial waters. A great deal of correspondence was exchanged with regard to that seizure. It was contended on the part of the United States authorities that as the vessel was seized in an open sea, that as the Bay of Fundy was an open sea, consequently the Canadian authorities had no right to make the seizure. It was contended by the British authorities that the Bay of Fundy was a bay, and that consequently the United States had no right to fish there. The matter was referred to that court. I will read article 2 of that treaty in which the procedure is set out:-
The high contracting parties agree that all claims on the part of corporations, companies, or private individuals, subjects of Her Britannic Majesty, upon the government of the United States, and all claims on the part of corporations, companies, or private individuals, citizens of the United States, upon the government of Her Britannic Majesty, which may have been presented to either government for it9 interposition with the other since the signature of the treaty of peace and friendship concluded between Great Britain and the United States of America at Ghent, on the 24th of December, 1814, and which yet remained unsettled, as well as any other claims which may be presented within the time specified in article 111 hereinafter, shall be

referred to two commissioners, to be appointed in the following manner, that is to say. One commissioner shall be named by Her Britannic Majesty, and one by the President of the United States. In ease of the death, absence or incapacity of either commissioner, or in the event of either commissioner omitting or ceasing to act as such, Her Britannic Majesty, or the President of the United States respectively shall forthwith name another person to act as commissioner in the place or stead of the coimmissioner originally named.
The commissioner shall then, and before proceeding to any other business, name some third person to act as arbitrator or umpire in any case or cases on which they may themselves differ in opinion. If they should not be able to agree upon the name of such third person, they shall each name a person; and in each and every case in which the com-tmissioners may differ in opinion as to the decision which they ought to give, it shall be determined by lot which of the two persons so named shall be the arbitrator or umpire in that particular case.
Well, under the provisions of that treaty the ' Washington ' claim was referred to the commissioners, who sat and heard the case. The majority of them decided that the Bay of Fundy was an open sea, and that consequently the ship's owner had a valid claim against the Canadian government. The Canadian authorities, or the British authorities, I do not know which, paid the $3,000 which were awarded as the amount of damages sustained by the seizure of the vessel.
Do I understand the hon. gentleman to say that the commissioners agreed on the $3,000 damages?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Two of them agreed, the majority.
I think the two commissioners did not agree, they absolutely disagreed, and the umpire gave the decision.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
The two commissioners disagreed, and the umpire sided with the American commissioner, which constituted a majority of the tribunal. On that point I may quote the conclusion of the award on page 217, which says:-
The conclusion is therefore in my mind irresistible that the Bay of Fundy is not a British bay, not a bay within the meaning of the word as used in the treaties of 1783 and 1818.
Now that was the question discussed, or reported, in the leading cases of international law at page 125. After mentioning the facts concerning the treaty of 1818 and the question of the Bay of Fundy, we read:-
It was subsequently held by a commission appointed to adjudicate on certain claims arising between the two countries, in the case of the schooner ' Washington ' which had been seized and declared forfeit for fishing in the Bay of Fundy, although at a distance of ten
miles from the shore, that that bay, which is over sixty ttniles wide and about one hundred and forty miles long, and which is as to one of its headlands within United States territory, did not constitute a territorial bay or water within the meaning of the exclusive clause of the treaty, but must be considered an open arm of the sea.
He quotes Scott, page 153, and Taylor, page 297. Now that was the situation until 1888, until the Chamberlain-Bayard treaty. My hon. friend from Digby has tried to-throw a great deal of responsibility on this government. As I have just shown, byreading the conclusion of the award, the tribunal decided that the Bay of F'undy, being an arm of the sea, the vessel could not be seized in its waters.
Is it not because they thought that declaration on the part of the referee, was an obiter dictum? '

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: My hon. friend will not dispute_ this fact. A seizure was made of a vessel in the Bay of Fundy. Is it true or not that what the arbitrators appointed to dispose of this question decided, was that ^.e.s.e^zure was illegal because it was made within the Bay of Fundy and the Bay of Fundy was an arm of the open sea?

I would like to point out to the minister that the tribunal were only asked to fix damages. They were not asked to determine whether the water upon which the seizure took place was an arm of the open sea or a bay. They were not international lawyers, they were not men trained in the law. Mr. Bates was a member of a banking firm who knew nothing about international law, but who did know how to assess damages. He fixed the damages at $3,000 and there his function ended. It was not part of his duty to determine whether the Bay of Fundy was a bay or part of the open sea.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I am afraid that the argument of my hon. friend is not founded on the facts as we find them on record. There was a claim made against the Canadian government as a result of the Canadian government having seized a vessel in the Bay of Fundy. There was not only a question of damages. If it had only been a question of damages we did not need to negotiate a treaty for the purpose of dealing with it. No treaty was necessary for that puropse, but the tribunal which adjudicated the case was called upon to decide whether the seizure was legal or illegal. The tribunal decided that as the seizure was made in the Bay of Fundy and as the Bay of Fundy was, in their mind, an arm of the open sea, damages were due to the owners of the vessel. If the Bay of Fundy had not been, in the mind of the authorities of the United States, open to question with regard to our jurisdiction why should

they have submitted this question to the court? They submitted it for the purpose of having a decision and the decision was rendered in their favour. That was the situation until 1888. In 1888 negotiations were entered into between the British, the Canadian and the United States: authorities for a new treaty with regard to the fisheries. Sir Charles Tupper represented the Canadian government, and he was also one of the negotiators who signed the treaty. My hon. friend states that this government has been derelict in its duty in connection with the fact that the Bay of Fundy has been excluded from the reference to the Hague Tribunal. But what does he say of Sir Charles Tupper who, in 1888 excluded the Bay of Fundy? My hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) who was an active member of the government at that time, approved of the treaty although it excluded the Bay of Fundy. Provision was made for the delimitation of hays in a certain way, but in that treaty which was made by Sir Charles Tupper, in the treaty which was approved by the Canadian parliament, in the treaty which was approved by the government of that time, it was stated formally that the Bay of Fundy was excluded. I suppose this fact will not be disputed by my hon. friend. Let me read to him the treaty of 1888. First I will take article 4:
At or near the following bays the limits of exclusion under Article 1, of the Convention of October 20, 1818, at points more than three marine miles from low water mark, shall be established by the following lines, namely.
Then they start with the Baie des Cha-leurs.
At the Baie des Chaleurs the line from the Light at Birch Point on Miscou Island to Macquereau Point light; at the Bay of Mira-michi, the line from the Light at Point Escu-minac to the light on the Eastern Point of Tabisintac Gully; at Egmont Bay, in Prince Edward Island, the line from the Light at Cape Egmont to the Light at West Point, and of St. Ann's Bay, in the province of Nova Scotia, the line from Cape Smoke to the Light at Point Anconi.
Then they speak of the bays in Newfoundland. Coming back to Canada they say:
At or near the following bays the limits of exclusion shall be three marine miles seaward from the following lines, namely:
At or near Barrington Bay, in Nova Scotia, the line from the Light on Stoddart Island to the Light on the South Point of Cape Sable, thence to the Light at Baccaro Point; at Chedabucto and St. Peter's bays, the line from Cranberry Island Light to Green Island Light, thence to Point Rouge; at Mira Bay, the line from the Light on the East Point of Scatari Island to the northeasterly point of Cape Morien; and at Placentia Bay, m Newfoundland, the line from Latine Point, on the eastern mainland shore, to the most southerly point of Red Island, thence by the most southerly point of Merasheen Island to the mainland.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
Long Island and Bryer Island, on St. Mary's Bay, in Nova Scotia, shall, for the purpose of delimitation, be taken as the coasts of such bay.
We see by the provisions of article 4 that they determine where the lines are to be drawn There is no word as to the Bay of Fundy. Why should not Sir Charles Tupper have provided also for the Bay of Fundy? Why was the Bay of Fundy excluded? Because I suppose the Americans contended, as they are contending to-day, that this question was settled by the correspondence of Lord Aberdeen and Mr. Everett, or by the treaty of 1853? At all events Sir Charles Tupper did not mention the matter at all in this treaty. But I go further and say-yes, he did mention it. If the Bay of Fundy is an open sea the question is disposed of, but if it is a bay what does he say in Article 3?
The three marine miles mentioned in Article 1, of the Convention of October 20, 1818, shall be measured seaward from low water mark; but at every bay, creek, or harbour, not otherwise specially provided for in this treaty, such three marine miles shall be measured seaward, from a straight line drawn across the bay, creek or harbour, in the part nearest the entrance at the first point where the width does not exceed ten marine miles.
What is the meaning of that? First, the treaty provides that some bays will have to be delimited in such and such a way. The Bay of Fundy is not included. Then, in article 3 where the bays are not specially mentioned they say that the three marine miles shall start from the point at which the bays narrow to a width of ten miles. What is the result? The result i3 that according to the treaty of 1888, the line of the Bay of Fundy will not be at a point opposite the county of Annapolis or opposite the county of Digby, but near the Basin of Minas and near Chignecto bay. That is absolutely clear and my hon.; friend will not dispute it, I think. How can the hon. gentleman say that the Minister of Justice was remiss in his duty in excluding the Bay of Fundy when his own former political leader Sir Charles Tupper when he was in power-and the hon. member for North Toronto was a member of his government-approved of the exclusion of the Bay of Fundy? In view of all this, is it not unfair and unjust to state that we have neglected our duty. Surely, it is plain from the correspondence exchanged between Lord Aberdeen and the governor of Nova Scotia in 1845, that the Bay of Fundy was excluded at that early date. The Americans contend it was excluded by the treaty of 1853, and in the treaty of 1888 we have a formal declaration that the Bay of Fundy, as to which my hon. friend (Mr. Jameson) says we have not fulfilled our duty, was also excluded.

The Minister of Marine apparently misses the point. In the case of the treaty of 1888 Canada was getting an undoubted title to the other bays as territorial waters, and was giving up or relaxing the question as to the Bay of Fundy out of the ten mile width. In the present case the whole subject matter of all the bays of Canada was to be arbitrated upon, and had the arbitration gone adversely to us we might have lost the whole of them. That was the difference between the two cases.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
Is it very likely that Sir Charles Tupper asked for the inclusion of the Bay of Fundy in 1888, and I suppose the representatives of the United States met that request with the same argument that was presented to us, namely, that they wanted the Bay of Fundy excluded from the reference. It was not mentioned in the treaty of 1888, and I have proven that that part of the Bay of Fundy about which the hon. gentleman is so anxious was declared to be absolutely an open sea, and that it should not be considered as a bay.

House resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when you left the Chair at six o'clock I was discussing the effect of the treaty of 1888. I showed that that treaty had virtually withdrawn the Bay of Fundy from any claim as to oui right to exclude American fishermen. In fact, as I have shown, some bays were withdrawn as being delimited in such and such a way, and no specific mention is made of the Bay of Fundy. There is a general clause in the treaty that the bays which are not specifically mentioned should be considered as territorial waters only where they are less than ten miles wide. That brings the Bay of Fundy, according to the treaty of 1888, among those which are open to American fishermen. From the mouth of the bay at Grand Manan to Chignecto, while Chig-necto bay and Minas Basin can be considered as territorial waters. Now, the leader of the opposition the other day put a question to my hon. friend the Minister of Justice in regard to Placentia bay, which is in Newfoundland territory. I do not know whether he intended to state that that bay was open from its mouth to its entire depth. From the way the question was put, I inferred that the hon. leader of the opposition believed that Placentia bay, by the treaty at Washington as well as by the Hague award, was closed from its mouth, that is, Point Bculpin to Gape -St. Mary. I do not know whether I interpreted clearly the opinion which my hon. friend expressed
or whether my inference from the question he put is correct.
I understand that for all these bays the line of demarcation, apart from the recommendations, is to be taken from headland to headland.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: My hon. friend is mistaken as to Placentia bay, which by the Hague award is declared to be open sea from the mouth marked by a line ' fro#? Latine point, on the eastern mainlands shore, to the most southerly point of Red island, thence by the most southerly point of Merasheen island to the mainland.' That means that the bay from the mouth to Merasheen point, which would be about 40 miles inside, is open sea. My hon. friend the other day showed me a map with a straight line drawn. This line is not the one determined by the Hague award as the line to be recommended.
My hon. friend knows that the award is one thing and the recommendations another. The same is true of all these bays, and Placentia bay does not stand alone in that respect.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
It is only a recommendation; but it is to be presumed that if the Bay of Fundy had been referred to the tribunal, the same judgment would have been rendered as in the case of Placentia bay, because at the mouth these bays are about the same width, namely, 45 miles, though the Bay of Fundy is muqh longer than the other. It is to be presumed that in such a case the tribunal would have recommended that the Bay of Fundy should be determined in the same way as it was determined in the treaty of i888. In that case all the other parts of the bay would be open to American fishermen. Though it is only a recommendation, I suppose that the two interested parties might expect that some day a definite agreement would be arrived at based on that recommendation; and so far the interested parties have been willing to act upon the recommendations that have been made. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice the other day raised the question that if we had succeeded in having the Bay of Fundy included in the reference, perhaps it would not have been especially advantageous t-o us, because it would have raised the question as to whether it could be considered a bay. As my hon. friend is aware, one of the headlands of this bay is American territory. If a line were drawn from Brier island to Grand Manan, and from Grand Manan to the other side, it would extend to American territory, and that would have raised a question which might- have embarrassed a settlement of the other question. For that reason I think mv hon. friend the Minister of Justice was fully justified in saying that in the interest of the whole
4G99

case it would perhaps be just as well to	leave the matter	as it is.
I say that the situation to-day, with regard to the Bay of Fundy, and which is the result of the treaty made in 1909, is far more favourable than what it was under the treaty of 1888. By the latter, the Bay of Fundy was opened to the American fishermen with the exception of its northern part, whereas by the present treaty, according to the agreement and according to the notes interchanged between Mr. Bryce and Mr. Bacon and according to the statement made in the United States Senate, it remains as it was before, and we have the same rights, advantages and privileges that we might have had formerly before the signing of this treaty. My hon. friend from Digby (Mr. Jameson), said that while the situation may not have been very advantageous undeT the treaty of 1888, still we had something in return. True, but we had nothing in return with regard to the Bay of Fundy. We obtained some provisions regarding the exchange of products, but, in so far as the Bay of Fundy itself was concerned, we got no compensation at all. Those who are trying to belittle what the government has done, will find that the treaty we made in 1909 is far more advantageous than the treaty made in 1888 by a former government. By this award we have gained a great deal, and I am sorry to find some of our hon. friends opposite trying to belittle its results. All Canadians who are anxious to see good relations between the two countries, should rejoice in the fact that we have already on two important matters, gained a great deal. We have gained first, the admission that we have the right to legislate with regard to those treaty coasts. That is a right which the Americans were denying us. They denied that we had the right to enact any legislation which might affect American fishermen fishing on the treaty coasts. On that point, the Hague award, which is the the Tesult especially of the work done by my hon. colleague the Minister of Justice, has given us a complete vindication. It declares that these are territorial waters, over which we have the sovereign control and with regard to which we consequently have the Tight to legislate. What else have we obtained? We know that, under the instructions given by Mr. Mitchell in 1870, when he was Minister of Marine and Fisheries, American fishing vessels could come and fish in our bays, provided they did not come within three miles of the coast or inside the bays. But what is the decision of the award in that respect? Take the Baie des Chaleurs, under the instructions given by Mr. Mitchell, when Minister of Marine and Fisheries in 1870, American fishermen Mr. BRODETTR.
could go throughout all that bay. But under this award, that bay will be closed from Berch Point on Miscou Island to Point Macquereau where the bay has a width of sixteen miles. Take the other bays, they will be clased to American fishermen inside limits as follows:
Miramichi, 14J miles.
Egmont I7J miles.
St. Peter's Bay, 18 miles.
Barrington Bay, 13 miles.
So you see the judgment^has given us great satisfaction and should' be acceptable to all those who are anxious to see good relations between the two countries.
I do not want to detain the House longer but I thought it necessary to put before the House all those facts which prove conclusively that those who try to belittle the work done by my hon. colleaghe the Minister of Justice (Sir Allen Aylesworth) and the results of the treaty, are anything but fair or reasonable. I may also say that we are greatly indebted to Mr. Bryce for the assistance he gave us and the efforts he made in order to bring about a settlement of this question, which during nearly a century was the cause of dissension between the two countries.
If the Bay of Fundy was not referred to the tribunal, that was not due to this government or the British authorities, but to the fact that the United States authorities refused absolutely to consent to its reference. UndeT the circumstances, would we have been justified, would my hon. colleague, the Minister of Justice, have been justified, in insisting on that point and thus preventing any reference as regards Canada and leaving solely the disputes between Newfoundland and the United States to be adjudicated by the Hague Tribunal without our being present at all? The questions which affected Newfoundland were not absolutely the same as those which concerned us. In some respects they were, but in others, they were not. Take the question of the Bay of Fundy, Newfoundland had not the same interest in that matter as we had; and if today we have succeeded in having this question settled once for all, it is due to the efforts made by those I have just mentioned and especially to the arduous work of the Minister of Justice. The matter has now been definitely settled. The United States had very good grounds for the position they took in the correspondence between Mr. Everett and Lord Aberdeen in 1845 and the treaty of 1853, and the award we have to-day is far more satisfactory than was the treaty of 1888. By that treaty, the Bay of Fundy was absolutely sacrificed, and that treaty was accepted by the government of that day and Sir Charles Tupper was one of those

most prominent in negotiating it. It was accepted also by the parliament of Canada. To-day, however, according to the notes interchanged, the question is still an open one, and in the meantime the Bay of Fundy is declared Canadian territory as it has always been considered by the British and Canadian authorities.

Mr. Speaker, this matter has been debated at such length that I do not intend to occupy very much of the time of the House in dealing with it. In fact, I rise more particularly for the purpose of correcting my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur) in respect of some arguments he used. Before doing that, however, I would like to say that it certainly is a matter for congratulation to both countries that this treaty of arbitration was entered into, and that a settlement of some at least of the outstanding questions between the two countries has been arrived at. I only hope that the day is not far distant when a wider treaty of arbitration between Canada and the United States will be consummated, so that all questions, not only those within the scope of the present treaty, but also questions of even graver import, may be referred to the arbitrament of The Hague Tribunal. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Sir Allen Ayles-worth) in the course of his speech on the 2nd of December last, went pretty fully into this question. I then congratulated my hon. friend and the government upon the fact that a settlement of some of these difficulties has been arrived at. I do not know that my congratulations would have been quite so warm if I had understood the award and the scope of the questions that were put as thoroughly as I think I do at present.
The Minister of Justice referred in terms of special commendation and eulogy to the work of Sir William Robson, now Lord Robson, who was one of the counsel for Great Britain before that tribunal. I have not a word to say in criticism of that: I have not the slightest doubt that Sir William Robson deserves all the encomiums that were heaped upon him with rather a lavish hand by the Minister of Justice. But I did, at the time, regard it as a little singular that several very able counsel who appeared on that occasion for Great Britain were hardly mentioned by the Minister of Justice. I have the honour of knowing Sir Robert Finlay, and happen to have been associated with him in the discussion of legal questions before the highest court of appeal on more than one occasion, and I should be surprised indeed if the argument of Sir Robert Finlay, delivered before The Hague Tribunal on behalf of Great Britain and in support of
the rights of Canada and Newfoundland were not worthy of just as high praise as that which was lavished upon Sir William Robson. I think also that a word of commendation might be said for the very earnest and devoted work which Mr. J. S. Ewart bestowed upon his duties both in connection with the preparation of the case and in the discussion of the rights of Canada and Newfoundland before that tribunal. Upon Mr. Ewart devolved a double duty. In the first place, he had a veT.y long work of investigation, to which he devoted his time and energy without stint, for, I think, eighteen months or two years before the hearing began. And not only in that respect did he do splendid work for his country, but any one who takes the trouble to read his argument delivered before that tribunal can see plainly for himself that it was an argument of great ability and of very high order.
I think also that it might not be amiss to congratulate the country that it had as a representative upon The Hague Tribunal a man of the public experience and distinguished legal ability of the present Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Canada. I venture to say that all that could properly be done in the interests of this country by the British representative upon that tribunal was done by Sir Charles Fitzpatrick on that occasion, and that this country owes not a little to his ability, his tact and his discrimination throughout the course of these proceedings.
I wish to speak for a moment upon one or two of the questions involved in the hearing. The first question was with regard to the rights of Great Britain over the territorial waters in which the fishermen of the United States, by the terms of the treaty, were to enjoy rights in common with the fishermen of this country and of Newfoundland. The United States put forward, as the hon. minister has very well said, an exceedingly extreme contention in that regard. They claimed the right not only to legislate in respect of these waters, but to enforce their legislation by having their own warships, if necessary, go into these waters to carry out the behests of the Congress of the United States. The government of this country had full rights in respect of the framing of the question which was submitted to the tribunal in that regard, and the Minister of Justice has made that absolutely plain. He said that the parties were so far apart from each other with regard to this question of the inherent sovereignty of Great Britain over these waters that no common understanding could be framed, and, therefore, each party was left to state its contention to be put forward before the tribunal. The contention of Great Britain was put forward in these words:

That the exercise of liberty to take fish referred to in the said article, which the inhabitants of the United States have for ever in common with the subjects of His Britannic Majesty, is subject without the consent of the United States, to reasonable regulation by Great Britain, Canada or Newfoundland in the forsm of municipal laws, ordinances or rules.
That is the contention on behalf of Great Britain, and it goes on to state examples of the regulations which might be made. Now, the tribunal sustained the able contention which had been put forward by Mr. Bryce on behalf of Canada and Newfoundland. 1 refer to the words of the Minister of Justice as given in Revised ' Hansard,' page 681:
When the award came to be pronounced on the 7th of September last, the tribunal adopted verbatim et litteratim the language which Mr. Bryce used two years ago in stating the British contention under this clause of the treaty.
I pause there for a moment to say that no hon. gentleman on this side, as I understood the argument, has said a word which could, in the slightest degree, reflect upon Mr. Bryce. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries has stated that some people in this country had apprehensions as to what might be the result when Mr. Bryce was named the British ambassador at Washington. So far as I am concerned, I have heard of none of these ' apprehensions ' and know of no one who entertained them, unless it be the Minister of Marine and Fisheries himself. I believe that Mr. Bryce has acted conscientiously and with ability and energy on behalf of the interests of the mother country and of Canada throughout the course of these difficulties at Washington. Any criticism of the form in which this treaty was made and in which these questions were- shaped is criticism not of Mr. Bryce, but of this government who were plainly responsible for every incident in these proceedings from the first to the last. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries cannot doubt that when he looks at the terms of the treaty itself, for it would have been impossible for Mr. Bryce, representing the mother country, to bind either Canada or Newfoundland in respect to this matter without the consent of Canada and Newfoundland.
The treaty in its terms provided that Great Britain had the distinct right, and therefore having the right, would be impelled to the duty of obtaining the consent of Canada and of Newfoundland in every case where the rights of Canada or of Newfoundland came into question.
Well, I was dealing with the mode in which this question had been framed, and with the award which was made thereon. Now the Minister of Justice has quoted a portion of the award which he says sets forth Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).

So up to the present time we have, in the first place, the reasons set forth plainly and distinctly by this tribunal, which confine the inherent power or sovereignty of Great Britain only within these limits, that regulations made with regard to these
fisheries must be bona fide and must not be in violation of the treaty. Then that is followed by a clear and distinct statement from this tribunal that the right of Great Britain is restricted by * the limitations and liabilities accepted in the special agreement, by the unequivocal position assumed by Great Britain in the presentation of its case before this tribunal,' showing that the inherent sovereignty of Great Britain must be cut down to the mere question as to whether these regulations are reasonable or not. And so in addition to that portion of the award which was read by my hon. friend the Minister of Justice, we find this in the operative part of the award, that part of the award which binds this country as well as the United States:
Regulations which are (1) appropriate or necessary for tbe protection and preservation of such .fisheries, or (2) desirable or necessary on grounds of .public order and morals without unnecessarily interfering with the fishery itself, and in both cases equitable and fair as between local and American fishermen, .and not so framed as to give unfairly an advantage to tbe former over the latter class, are not inconsistent with the obligation to execute tbe treaty in good faith, and are, therefore, reasonable and not .in violation of the treaty.
For the decision of .the question whether a regulation is or is not reasonable, as being or not in accordance with the disposition of the treaty and not in violation thereof, the treaty of 1818 contains no special provision. By reason, however, of the form in which question 1 is put, and by further reason of the admission of Great Britain by her counsel before this tribunal that it is not now for either of the parties to the treaty to determine the reasonableness of any regulation made by Great Britain, Canada or Newfoundland, the reasonableness of such regulation, if contested, must be decided not by either of the parties, but by an impartial authority in accordance .with the principles hereinabove laid down, and in the manner preposed in the recommendations made by the tribunal in virtue of Article 4 of the agreement,
The result of that, Mr. Speaker, seems to me capable of being stated in a very few words. In the one case the power of Great Britain-that is of Canada and Newfoundland-to regulate the fisheries is subject only to the qualification that the regulation must be bona fide and must not be in violation of the treaty. That is a position that we could have maintained if this question had been prepared for the tribunal in the way in which the government should have proposed it. In other words, if the contention which, as the Minister of Justice declares, was put forward by Mr. Bryce, had been maintained in the questions submitted by the government to that tribunal the part of this award which I first quoted would have been the only part to which the tribunal would have given utterance, and we would not have

been put in a position to which I shall now devote one or two words. In the one case, the power of Great Britain (i.e. Canada and Newfoundland) to regulate the fisheries would be subject only to the qualification that the regulation must be bona fide and must not be in violation of the Treaty. The other case, the case that confronts us actually at the present time, is in which the government stated our position, we have come down to the question of . reasonable regulations which will undoubtedly be considered from the actual conditions confronting the United States fishermen. Under the award the United States can object to the reasonableness of any regulation that we may make and can insist upon a hearing and a decision of the Hague Tribunal, or some other body constituted under the decree of that tribunal. The right to regulate has in effect passed from Canada and Newfoundland, who possessed it by virtue of the inherent sovereignty of Great Britain in these waters, and it has passed to a foreign tribunal which would undoubtedly deal with this question in a spirit of compromise and cut something out of any code of regulations however reasonable. We have in effect abrogated our sovereignty over these waters in this respect. An exercise of our inherent sovereignty to regulate the fisheries can always be questioned by the United States and decided by a tribunal in which we have only one voice out of many. The Minister of Justice will see how remarkable a difference there is between the one position and the other. In the one case at any time, under our inherent sovereignty, we could have adopted any regulation whatever provided that regulation was bona fide and not in violation of the treaty of 1818. That right, by reason of the form in which the question was put and by reason of the decree of the tribunal founded upon that question, has been cut down to a pure question as to whether or not our regulations are reasonable having regard to the conditions which confront the American fisherman, and whatever regulations we may make can be questioned by the government of the United States, and when so questioned must be dealt with by a tribunal in which we have only one voice out of many. I think that is an unfortunate position, and I think it is a position which was entirely unnecessary. I am adopting in that regard the statement of the Minister of Justice himself who says that the portion of the award which he read-and he did not read the qualification-and which maintains the inherent sovereignty of Great Britain over these waters, was put forward by Mr. Bryce; and after it had been put forward by Mr. Bryce I see no reason Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).

Now, I come to another question-the question of bays and harbours. The Minister of Justice seems to be under the impression that in so far as that is concerned some new and important rule of international law was settled. I venture to doubt that with great deference to the Minister of Justice, for whose ability and experience I have the utmost possible respect. As I understand the award it did not settle any new principle of international law. I have the minister's own language, but I will not stop just now to read it. He seemed to think not only that a new and important rule of international law had been settled, but that the tribunal, basing its decision upon the argument of Sir William Robson, had determined a different rule of international law for the waters adjoining the coast of this continent from that which has prevailed in Europe. With all deference to my hon. friend the Minister of Justice and with hesitation owing to the view that he has expressed to the contrary, I venture to differ from that opinion. As I understand the award it simply construed the words of the treaty of 1818, taking into consideration the circumstances and conditions when it was made. The word ' bays ' in that treaty had to be construed either as a term of international law-that is in what one might call the juristic sense, or it had to be construed otherwise as an ordinary geographical term, in the popular sense, in other words, as a cartological term. The tribunal simply adopted the latter construction. They said that when the negotiators of the treaty of 1818 used the word ' bays ' they simply used it in the popular and geographical sense at the time and I do not find any new rule of international law laid down. Perhaps I might refer for one moment to what the Minister of Justice has said in that regard. He said that Sir William Robson had made a very novel and beautiful argument founded on the research that he had made into former treaties, and that his argument led irresistibly to the conclusion that a different rule of international law prevailed in North America from that which obtained in the rest of the world. The tribunal, as he claimed, had decided accordingly, and the tribunal in so deciding had laid down a new and important rule of international law. I am not giving the exact language of the Minister of Justice because I do not wish to take up the time of the House in listening to long quotations, but I am giving the effect of his statement on the subject in December la3t. Bat Sir William Robson does not appear, as Mr. Ewart

has said, to have conducted any particular research into these treaties, because they had all 'been set out in the Appendix to the British case from pages 1 to 24. I looked at this volume only the other day, and I saw that they are all there. This Appendix was prepared a year before Sir William Robson made his argument. They had been referred to in this very argument by previous counsel before Sir William Robson made his excellent argument before the tribunal. I do not think that the tribunal has laid down any different rule of international law in respect to America from that which exists elsewhere. I have the award in my hand, and I shall forbear from reading to the House the reasons of the award which lead me to arrive at that conclusion. There is only one possible passage in the award that can afford the slightest foundation for the view which my hon. friend the Minister of Justice expressed in the House, but if you take that particular paragraph which is to be found at the bottom of page 35 of the edition I have in connection with other reasons which are to be found from pages 31 to 35, it does not seem to me that you can reasonably come to the conclusion that the Minister of Justice reached in that regard. I have not one word to say in deprecation of the eulogiums which the Minister of Justice lavished upon Sir William Robson, but in so far as I understand the real character of this award, the real meaning of the award it does not justify the view that my hon. friend the Minister of Justice seems to entertain.
The Minister of Marine seems to deprecate the discussion of this award, but it was the Minister of Justice who began the discussion in this House on the 2nd of December, and because two hon. members on this side representing constituencies that are directly affected by this award put forward their views on it with great ability and fairness, the Minister of Marine thinks party politics have been introduced into the question. Well, the same hon. gentleman was not very slow to endeavour to make party capital out of the French treaty, and I should think he would be the last person to make the insinuation he has made. I congratulate the hon, member for Digby (Mr. Jameson) for bringing this question to the attention of the House. It was his clear duty to take that course. The Minister of Marine put forward some very remarkable arguments with regard to the exclusion of the Bay of Fundy from the reference, and I may say that it would appear to me that he devoted too much of his speech to advancing the favourable points in the American contention rather than the favourable points in the Canadian contention. It was not necessary that the minister should do
that because from the first to last throughout the negotiations, the preparation of the case, and the argument before the tribunal it is very apparent that the negotiators and the counsel for the United States in every single instance put forward their claims in the most extreme form, which in my opinion was not done in the same way by those representing this country. The hon. gentleman attached undue importance to the award made in 1854 for damages on account of the seizure of the ship * Washington.' If that decision has the far reaching effect attributed to it by the Minister of Marine it would have controlled not only the Bay of Fundy but every one of these bays, and yet all the other bays brought within the scope of the arbitration have been declared by the tribunal to be British territorial waters so far as the fishermen of the United States are concerned. The real explanation of the ' Washington' case was given by Mr. Dana interrupting Mr. Thompson in the argument before the fishery tribunal in Halifax, in 1877, when he said:
This subject was referred to a commission and the commission decided, not on general grounds but on the grounds that one headland was on the American territory.
This vessel was seized outside of the line which we claim to-day. If you take a very extreme limit it may be said that one headland is on the coast of Maine and the other is on the coast of Nova Scotia, but the later contention, as I understand it is, that you must draw a line between Canadian territory in Nova Scotia and Canadian territory in New Brunswick. However, I will not waste more time on that point.
The Minister of Marine derives great comfort from the Chamberlain-Bayard treaty of 1888, when dealing with the Bay of Fundy, and he says that by that treaty the Bay of Fundy was excluded and that all the other bays were dealt with along the lines of the recommendations made by the Hague Tribunal. But, the distinction is obvious beyond question. Let us grant for the sake of argument-I have not investigated the negotiations to speak definitely with regard to them-but let us grant that Mr. Chamberlain and Sir Charles Tupper agreed that in consideration of having the sovereignty of great Britain recognized in respect of all those other bays, they would not make any further claim in respect to the Bay of Fundy in which the American fishermen had been enjoying rights under the relaxation allowed by Lord Aberdeen in 1845. That simply amounts to this: That they -were getting a certain distinct, clear advantage in consideration of not depart-

ing from the relaxation of 1845, but surely the Minister of Marine knows that the Chamberlain-Bayard treaty was not the foundation of this agreement for arbitration. Can he not see the distinction between that case and this? In that case, rights which were disputed by the Americans were made absolutely secure to us and we did not press for the discontinuance of the relaxation which had already been granted in respect to the Bay of Fundy. In 1909 the situation was entirely different because then we were not securing undisputed rights in respect to all these bays. The Americans put forward their extreme contention that the three-mile limit and that only was to be recognized in respect to all these bays. Therefore, when the whole question of right was being opened up in respect to these bays that were secure to us under the treaty of 1888, why should not the question of right be opened up with respect to the Bay of Fundy? Why was it that that which the Americans had agreed to give in 1888 they were at liberty to depart from under this agreement, and that which we had agreed to give up under the treaty of 1888 we had not the right to open up, but had to let it remain secure to the United States under the provisions of this agreement. The distinction is as plain as a pikestaff; it need only be mentioned so that any one may understand it. If the two nations had taken the treaty of 1888 as a basis the Minister of Marine would have some ground for his argument, but in as much as everything the Americans were supposed to concede by the treaty of 1888 was left open under the terms of this reference there was not the slightest reason for not contending that the Bay of Fundy should also be included and our rights asserted in respect to it. Because the practical distinction for the purpose of this fishery between coasts and bays and the exceptional conditions pertain-Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).

For the moment just let me refer to the value of the fisheries in the Bay of Fundy. From a statement made up by
