Why should it not have been determined? The Minister of Justice and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries have given us the American contention in that regard, and have referred us over and over again to the letter written by Lord Aberdeen in 1845. I think they have been answered in that regard by hon. gentlemen who have preceded me; but let me point out this. If that was a good ground for giving up the Bay of Fundy, it might have been a good ground for giving up something else. Let us look at that for a moment. We find that the instructions issued by Mr. Mitchell, Minister of Marine and Fisheries in 1870, were first framed in this way;
Until further instructed, therefore, you will not interfere with any American fishermen, unless found within three miles of the shore, or within three miles of a line drawn across the mouth of a bay or creek which is less than ten geographical miles in width. In the case of any other bay, as the Bay of Chaleurs, for example, you will not admit any United States fishing vessel or boat, or any American fishermen, inside of a line drawn across at that part of such bay where its width does not exceed ten miles.
On June 6,	1876, Lord Grenville telegraphed to the Governor General as follows :
Her Majesty's government hopes that the United States fishermen will not be for the present prevented from fishing, except within three miles of land, or in bays which are less than six miles broad at the mouth.
The result was that the Hon. Peter Mitchell modified his instructions on the 27th of June, 1870, making the last paragraph read:
In the case of any other bay, as Bay des Chaleurs, for example, you will not interfere with any United States "fishing vessel or boat, or any American fishermen, unless they are found within three miles of the shore.
As far as I understand the practice, from that time up to the present the instructions then given by Mr. Mitchell have been followed. So that if there was good ground for giving up the Bay of Fundy by reason of Lord Aberdeen's letter of 1845, there was equally good ground for giving up the Bay of Chaleurs and every other bay, because these instructions had been definitely given at the request of the British government that American fishermen were not to be interfered with, unless found fishing within three miles of the shore. Further than that, with respect to the Bay of Fundy, and the strong view expressed as to Lord Aberdeen's language in 1845, let me refer to the position taken by Mr. Phelps in 1886.
Mr. Phelps, the American Minister at the Court of St. James that year, after stating the regret of the United States government that the Royal assent had been given to the Act of this parliament passed in the previous year, touching fishing by foreign vessels, proceeded to state as follows:
It lias been pointed out in my note to Lord Iddesleigh above mentioned that the three-mile limit referred to in this Act is claimed by the Canadian government to include considerable portions of the high seas, such as the Bay of Fundy, the Bay of Chaleurs and similar waters, by drawing the line from headlands to headlands. And that American fishermen have been excluded from those waters accordingly.
This indicates in the clearest possible way that whatever the contention of the British government was regarding the Baie des Chaleurs in 1886-7, it was asserting the same contention as respects the Bay of Fundy.
My hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Sir Allen Aylesworth) asked how we could have expected the authorities of the United States to enter into any agreement regarding the Bay of Fundy when they were perfectly satisfied with the position as it was. Of course they were. They had been fishing in that bay without restriction or interference; and if they could persuade this government to be foolish enough to submit the question of right in respect to all the other bays and leave-nut the Bay of Fundy, they naturally would be extremely well satisfied. They would then have the opportunity of making good their claims in respect of all the other bays, and Great Britain would have no opportunity whatever of making good her claims in respect of the Bay of Fundy. There was no need for my hon. friends opposite to assure us that the United States authorities were perfectly satisfied to leave that matter as it was. We understand that, but the question is could the people of. Canada be perfectly satisfied

that, when this question of right was put forward, our government should have consented that the Bay of Fundy-perhaps the most important bay on the coast of Canada-should be absolutely put aside and not be submitted to this tribunal. The treaty of arbitration, under which this agreement was entered into, gave no excuse whatever for excluding the Bay of Fundy. Article 1 says:
Differences which may arise of a legal nature or relating to the interpretation of treaties existing between the two contracting parties and which it may not have been possible to settle by diplomacy, shall be referred to the permanent court of arbitration established at the Hague by the convention of the 29th July, 1899, provided nevertheless that they do not affect the vital interests, the independence, or the honour of the two contracting states, and do not concern the interest of third parties.
There you have a definite, distinct agreement to submit the differences. Was there not a difference between the government of Canada and the United States with respect to our rights in the Bay of Fundy? Was there not exactly the same difference between the government of Great Britain, as represented by the Canadian government for the time being, with respect to that bay as there was with respect to the Baie des Chaleurs? What was the difference between the two cases? Absolutely none, and the treaty called for a submission of such differences.
My hon. friends the Minister of Justice (Sir Allen Aylesworth) and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur) did seem to rely to an undue extent on Lord Aberdeen's letter. True, the Minister of Justice said in December last that:
The result of the argument made during the present summer and the award pronounced two months ago has been to uphold to the fullest extent the British contention, and to demonstrate I think, that if the concession regarding the Bay of Fundy had not been made in 1845, that bay, as well as the other large bays of our maritime provinces, would to-day be declared British territorial waters.
I have dealt with the character of the relaxation very briefly, but I would like to read just in this connection the reasoning of the tribunal itself with regard to relaxations of a similar character. The counsel for the United States had put forward an argument based on a relaxation by Great Britain of its rights with regard to other bays, and the tribunal disregarded that claim for this reason:
Because neither should such relaxations of this claim, as are in evidence, be construed as renunciations of it; nor should omissions to enforce the claim in regard to bays as to which no controversy arose, be so construed. Such a construction by this tribunal would not only be intrinsically inequitable but in-Mr. BOKDEN (Halifax).
ternationally injurious; in that it would discourage conciliatory diplomatic transactions and encourage the assertion of extreme claims in their fullest extent;
As has been well pointed out by my hon. friends who preceded me on this side (Mr. Jameson and Mr. Maddin) the relaxation of Great Britain in that regard was_ not accepted by the United States subject to the stipulation which accompanied it. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Sir Allen Aylesworth) has construed that stipulation in a very different sense from that placed upon it by my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries because, quoting from revised 'Hansard,' page 671, I find him using this language in referring to the opinion given by the Attorney General of Nova Scotia, the Hon. James W. Johnson:
That opinion having been pronounced by the responsible law officers of the Crown of that day, the colonists of Nova Scotia, I have no doubt, felt their case immensely strengthened, and thought they would have behind them all the prestige and power of the British government itself in defending the claim they were making to the Bay of Fundy as part of their territorial waters. But in 1845, the Lord Aberdeen of that day, then Foreign Secretary of Great Britain, wrote a letter which had been prepared as a piece of diplomatic correspondence, after the most careful and matured consideration, in which while affirming the right of the colonies, while standing upon the opinion which had been expressed by their legal advisers and by the legal advisers of the British government, none the less, on the part of His Majesty's government, as a pure matter of grace and concession, he expressed his willingness to forego, so far as the Bay of Fundy was concerned, the extreme right of the British subject in that regard, and assented to the use, by the fishermen of the United States, of the fisheries in the Bay of Fundy, in common with the inhabitants of the British colonies, upon the stipulation that as to the remainder of the maritime coasts of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Quebec, the claims of United States fishermen should cease.
That is the plain, distinct construction placed upon that letter by my hon. friend the Minister of Justice, and it is a construction entirely inconsistent with that placed upon it by my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur).
We are asked: What injury has been done by not including the Bay of Fundy? But an equally pertinent question would be:	What injury would have been done
by including it? My hon. friends the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries argued that the British case would have been greatly handicapped by the inclusion of the Bay of Fundy. As I understand it, that supposed handicap would have arisen either by reason of the shape of the bay, the different

character of the bay or by reason of the letter of Lord Aberdeen in 1845. So far as
the character of the bay is concerned, any one who examines it upon the map can see that just as powerful an argument could have been made with respect to that bay on the part of Great Britain as with respect to Placentia bay, or any of the others. And any one who examines the argument made before the tribunal and the reasons given by it will see that two great factors entered into consideration.
One was the width of the bay at the mouth, and the other the depth of the bay. Taking it from shore to shore across Grand Manan, it does not seem to be wider than Placentia bay. But the depth of the Bay of Fundy is greater. Placentia bay is only 70 miles deep until you reach the ten mile line, whereas the Bay of Fundy is at least 100 miles deep before you reach the ten mile line. Therefore, so far as the character of the Bay of Fundy is concerned, there is no reason to differentiate it from the other bays that were brought before the tribunal. We are told that it would have been a handicap had the Bay of Fundy been brought into the discussion, that the British argument would not have been so strong and cogent as it was. As a matter of fact, it was brought before the tribunal. The letter of Lord Aberdeen, written in 1845, was canvassed before the tribunal. Bates' decision was canvassed. Everything was urged by the Americans at this hearing which could possibly have been urged by them if the Bay of Fundy had been included in the arbitration. The Minister of Justice practically admits this. In one part of his speech, he says that if the Bay of Fundy had been included, some great disadvantage would have been sustained. Bat in another part of his speech he admitted that everything was brought in question with regard to that bay. At page 4707 of the Unrevised 'Hansard,' he said:
I venture to think our position was better before the tribunal without any reference to the Bay of Fundy being included in the matters for decision, the arrangement being that nothing in the proceedings should prejudice our claims with reference to the Bay of Fundy or the claims of the United States in reference to the Bay of Fundy.
Then, he says, at page 4696:
The attitude of both parties in the previous years in the course of the prolonged diplomatic discussion, while it related immediately to the Bay of Fundy, had the most important possible bearing upon the general question of the interpretation of this clause of the treaty, and just for that reason every word, I may say every letter, of that long diplomatic correspondence was scrutinized with the utmost care, was presented before the tribunal and was discussed over and over again on both sides of the question by the 149
various counsel who were concerned in the case.
So, as a matter of fact, we had all the handicap in regard to the Bay of Fundy that we could possibly have had under any circumstances, and we had not the advantage of obtaining an award with regard to that very important body of water. The injury to Canada to-day is in not having the question decided one way or the other. Hon. members opposite have. spoken of the importance of having this question settled. Well, is it settled to-day? Have they given up our rights in the Bay of Fundy? Do they stand in the position in which they seem to have stood in these negotiations, that we have absolutely relinquished all our territorial rights in the Bay of Fundy, though under the terms of the tribunal, we have absolute rights in these territorial waters? Has the government of this country given up the Bay of Fundy, with its marvellous fisheries, in which more than five thousand men are engaged, in which more than $2,000,000 of capital is invested, and whose annual production is nearly $3,000,000? Have they given up our claims with respect to that? If so, why has the claim of this country been abnegated in regard to the Bay of Fundy when it has been asserted before this tribunal in regard to other territorial waters? The injury is in not having the question of jurisdiction settled. That has two aspects. In the first place, it is in the interest of friendship between the two countries, that the question should be settled. I offered my congratulations to the government in the early days of the session, that many questions had been settled. It had not then dawned upon me that the Bay of Fundy had been excluded in the way it has been. It is in the interest of good relations between the countries that it should be settled; and I should have thought that, unless the government propose to absolutely abandon all our claims in regard to that bay, they would have persisted for that very reason even if they thought we had not a good case, upon having the Bay of Fundy included in that arbitration, in order that we might have a definite and clear decision in regard to the rights of the fishermen of both countries in these waters. What does the government propose to do about it? The Minister of Justice said, in one part of his speech, that he was glad the Bay of Fundy had not been included, and in another part, he said that wre stand in a better position in regard to it than before. If it be true, as he stated, then the tribunal has confirmed in the most complete manner and to the fullest possible extent our contention with respect to these bays, including the Bay of Fundy, what does the government propose to do about



it? Are they going to open up the matter again with the United States? Or have they estopped themselves from doing this, by neglecting to have this bay included in this reference ? I do not know the exact character of the negotiations in that regard. They have not been brought down in the form of written documents, other than the memoranda which have been read. But I do most sincerely trust that no steps taken by this government in that respect, will have precluded this country from asserting its rights, in this connection.
One other question only I would like to allude to. Having regard to the decision of this tribunal upon the second question, the position of Canada and Newfoundland acting jointly seems to me to be a very strong one. Question 2 was as follows:
Have the inhabitants of the United States, while exercising the liberties referred to in said article, a right to employ as (members of the fishing crews of their vessels persons not inhabitants of the United States?
I understand perfectly that this is a question which touches Newfoundland more than it touches Canada, but, I take it that the answer to that question, coupled with the control of the bait supply, made Great Britain-that is, Canada and Newfoundland -complete, masters of the situation. The control of the bait supply is a very important thing indeed. My hon. friend expresses surprise and disappointment because the tribunal did not proceed to deal with the reasonableness of certain regulations made by Canada and the United States.
I touched upon the main question in connection with that, and I pointed out that the tribunal made a certain disposition by which it would be determined whether any regulation was or was not reasonable. I am inclined to think if the Minister of Justice had taken the trouble to make himself a little better acquainted with the situation than he seems to have been, he might not have expressed so much surprise nor so much disappointment with the tribunal at the course it did take in that regard. I will not say anything more than that. As a matter of fact, I think that after the government had given away our case to some extent, as it seems to me they did, by the shape in which they put the question touching the reasonableness of regulation, it was exceedingly fortunate for us that the tribunal took the course it did take. As a result of that, Newfoundland has still the right to control its bait supply; and the tribunal has decided that Canada and Newfoundland have the right of control over their own citizens being employed upon United States fishing vessels. If my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and other members of the government will put these two things together Mr. BORDEN (Halifax). .
and see what they amount to, I think eventually they might come to the conclusion that so far as these fisheries are concerned we have the situation in our own hands, and that the fish of the maritime provinces would at no distant day have entered the markets of the United States free of duty, even if no reciprocity treaty had been made. That is the conclusion I have come to after considerable study of this award, and of what it means to the people of this country and the people of Newfoundland.
Now I am glad that these matters were submitted to this tribunal. I regret the form in which some of them were submitted. I regret that the government did not follow the example of the United States, and put its contentions in every respect at the highest point at which they could have been maintained. They failed to do that, and the result has not been helpful to the cause of Canada. However, it is a desirable thing that these disputes should be settled, I rejoice that some at least have been settled. I hope the government will take the opportunity at no distant date of announcing to the House what its policy will be with regard to the Bay of Fundy, in view of the fact that the waters of that bay are territorially the waters of Great Britain, under the reasons advanced by this tribunal, and under the award based upon those reasons.

Having failed at a previous stage of this sitting to say a few wiords on this subject, I will ask the House to listen to me now, and I do so the more readily because I seldom take up the tiine of this House. I would not have returned to the subject were it not that I consider the editorial criticism in the Ottawa ' Citizen ' of my remarks as unfair and unjust, and that I should reply to them. There seems to be a feeling in the city that nobody outside has a right to discuss this question at all. The Ottawa ' Citizen ' insinuates that I made remarks unfair to Ottawa. A gentleman speaking at a meeting on Friday evening, I think it was, and who I believe is a reporter in this House, said that I put it over Ottawa too strong. Now if my language was too strong, what must we say of the language of the gentleman who addressed a meeting n the Young Mens' Christian Association on Saturday to which I listened. My remarks were as the moonlight to the sunlight, or as water to wine compared with theirs, or as water to hot Scotch compared to what was given out there. I think that I, as well as every other member of this House of Commons, has a perfect right to take part in a discussion of the water we are compelled to drink. If it is a family

row in the city of Ottawa, I represent here a family of 225 persons who are obliged to drink the water of the Ottawa. So far as I am concerned personally, I do not drink it, and never have since I first came here. I tried it twice, and I was so sick each time that I have abstained from it ever since. I have lived in this city during the last six years as much of the time as I have lived in Nova Scotia, and I claim the right to criticise the nature of the water we are given to drink. Coming back to this editorial, the editor says that I have made an unfortunate attack, and given much publicity, ' unfair publicity,' I believe he says, to the conditions of the Ottawa water supply. Why, Sir, before I had ever said a word, the ' Citizen ' itself had been spreading the news from Vancouver to Halifax. There was hardly a paper but that has published news in regard to the typhoid epidemic at Ottawa. Then the ' Citizen,' after helping along this publicity, turns around and blames me for the few gentle remarks I made here. It says:
Dr. Black asserts that it is known where the present outbreak has originated. If it is not a matter of common knowledge, and Dr. Black is not using the city fairly by withholding such information particularly at this time. We may be getting poisoned, as Dr. Black intimates, but we can still conscientiously plead that we don't know how any more than at the beginning of the present outbreak.
Well, I regret very much the ignorance of the editor of the ' Citizen.' The report published in Toronto of the health officer who has examined the Ottawa water, says that the typhoid epidemic comes from that water. Dr. Bryce at a meeting on Friday says:
It is a water epidemic pure and simple. He placed the responsibility entirely on the water.
Dr. McCullough says :
The chief cause of the typhoid in Ottawa is the water.
Now I think these are pretty good proofs that somebody besides Dr. Black knows the location. I was going to say, when I was stopped as trespassing on the orders of the day, that there were four and possibly five modes of carrying typhoid. First, there is the water, which is the great carrier. Typhoid is a water-borne disease. Every man who has studied public health knows that typhoid is essentially a waterborne disease. Secondly, it is carried by milk, and it gets into the milk only by being carried there, by washing the milk cans or milk pitchers in polluted water that has not been boiled.
It might be introduced into the milk by a fly dropping into it and carrying the poison with it. That is No. 2, and No. 3 is, the fly 149i
which carries the bacillus from the excrement to our food dropping it into the milk pitcher, the sugar bowl, candy or anything else. The fourth is contagion where an individual comes in contact with a person affected with typhoid. Possibly the fifth and probably the fifth, is wind-carried bacilli. This can be excluded because the earth is^ covered with snow at the present time. Flies can be excluded because there are not many around Ottawa at the present time. I am afraid there are some on the man who wrote that editorial. Milk is certified in Ottawa as pure. Now, by the laws of exclusion, we come back to one cause and one only. We must take the analysis of the water, and, taking the opinion of Dr. Bryce and of Dr. McCullough-not ndJie we must come to the conclusion that the source of this disease is in the river. If it is not, in heaven's name, why is everybody crying out to have the water purified? Ottawa is trying to do the impossible. You cannot run two trains in opposite directions on one track without meeting disaster and death. You cannot soil and pollute the water of the river with the by-products of the human body and drink the same water without disaster and death. There may be let-ups, there may be periods when nobody is being killed, but every once in a while there will be an outbreak such as we have now. Let us see what is the history of Ottawa in regard to this very thing; this attempting to pollute the water and to drink it also. I have not had a great deal of time to look up the public health reports but I have looked at some of them. In 1895 there were 195 cases of typhoid in Ottawa, and in 1889-22 years agao-there were 2,000 cases. Have there been uny since those years? What has there been between those years? Here is a sentence in the official report of the medical health officer for Ottawa. He sadly says ' typhoid fever is a yearly visitor to swell our death-roll.' That is the health offcer's report. 1 think that with the statement that we have had typhoid every year and with the records of the other years, it is about time that Ottawa had decided that it is doing the impossible, that it is trying to drink water that is being polluted. It is further giving to all the communities down below the poison from here. The result is that typhoid has broken out at Rockland. I think I have shown my justification for the remarks I have made, that the poison is properly located, that the river has been polluted for years and that somebody else started the publicity before I did. I have no advice to give to Ottawa, but there are only two things for Ottawa to do-stop having this river polluted or take the water from somewhere else. London, England, has a river flowing through it but it never thinks of drinking the water. It goes away back to the principality of Wales for its.

supply. New York has the Hudson river flowing past it, but it never attempts to tap that source of supply; it goes fifty miles away for water. Vancouver does the same. Yet, we adopt the slip-shod trick of our forefathers, who took their water wherever they could get it handiest without knowledge. That has been tried by different cities all over the continent of America. The result has been thousands and thousands of cases of typhoid fever, and the cities all along the great rivers, such as the Ohio, Mississippi and the Missouri, have wakened up to the fact that it is impossible to pollute their water and drink it too. They have gone elsewhere for pure water or they have gone to enormous expense in counteracting the pollution that has been going on in the rivers.
We are not half as wise in these things as the ancients were. I might quote from Dr. Montizambert's speech on Saturday in saying that 2,500 years ago the Romans would not drink the water from the Tiber but they built that magnificent aqueduct that still has water flowing through it. Jerusalem, he also stated, went away where it could get pure water and brought it at great expense through an aqueduct. You cannot pollute the water and drink it without disaster, and Ottawa must either purify the water above the city or she must go somewhere else to get pure water. If the pollution above the town is stopped the pollution at the town must be stopped in fairness to those below. I am very sorry to have had this much to say but I thought it was only right that I should say this in justice to myself considering the way in which my remarks had been received by the ' Citizen.'

Mr. Speaker, I must say that I think that the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Black) has been discharging a great and important public duty. I think that he deserves the gratitude, not only of the members of this House, but of the citizens of Ottawa. We are all proud of the national capital and we want it to have a good name. I do not think, however, that attempting to conceal the unfortunate conditions which exist is going to do any good. The only thing to do is to correct them if possible. To-day the typhoid outbreak has actually reached such a state that the question is asked by people throughout the whole city: Who will be next? If the discussions in the House and the discussions in the press can do anything I think that the movement which has been set on foot and which has been so much stimulated by the action of the hon. member for Hants will work for that end, and I think he deserves, as I have said before, the thanks of the House and the citizens of Ottawa for the action which he has taken in that regard.

speakeroldname: Hon. WM. PUGSLEY (Minister of Public Works).
speechtext:
I endeavoured to convey that the flag should be flown daily on all public buildings under the control of my department in border cities and towns, and at the principal seaports, and also, upon all public buildings on special days. I do not know that it has ever been the custom to fly a flag upon the Intercolonial Railway buildings on special days, and the Militia Department has certain rules which govern the display of flags on the buildings under its control. I issued instructions that the flag should be flown upon all the post offices and custom houses on St. David's day as well as upon other special days, and that in border cities and towns the flag should be flown every day in the year on these buildings. Some of the officials did not apparently understand the order with reference to St. David's day, which would account for the flag not being raised on the post office in St. John on that day, although it was displayed on the custom house. I have had a peremptory order sent out by the chief architect, and I do not think it will

be misunderstood in future. I was sorry that on St. David's day the flag was not hoisted on the Ottawa post office, but there was some misunderstanding on the part of the official whose duty it was to attend to the matter. As soon as my attention was called to the fact that it was not flying on the parliament building on St. David's day I gave orders which were at once attended to. I trust that in future the orders will be well understood.
I am glad to hear the statement of the minister in regard to the buildings over which he has control. What is the rule in regard to the militia buildings?

I am under the impression that the flying of the flag on forts and military buildings has some special significance. I do not think that either in England or in Canada it is customary to fly the flag from forts or military buildings as on other public buildings. However, I will get the information and let my hon. friend know at some later date.

I think the flag flies from forts every day they are occupied or garrisoned, and of course Fort Dufferin is only occasionally garrisoned. On military stores buildings and such, I should think the flag ought to be displayed as on other public buildings.
There are certain regulations governing such matters and I do not think there is any intention of changing them.

What is the reason for increasing the clerical staff?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The increased business of the department. I might read, for the information of the committee, a memorandum which was placed in my hands to-day by some of the officers of the department, as it bears on this point. First, there is a memorandum to the commissioner from the deputy commissioner, which says:
I again, desire to bring to your attention the necessity for additional assistance and accommodation for the staff of this branch of the department. The work has increased during the past ten years from 471 per cent under one heading to as high as 734 per cent under another; and there is every prospect of it becoming heavier, as settlers begin to apply for patent for the homestead and other entries made since immigration assumed its present large proportions.
It is of course impossible to provide more staff without somewhere to put them. At the present moment we are crowded to a degree which is not only embarrassing and detrimental to the work but absolutely dangerous to the health of the clerks. Our sick list during the past year has been very large, and no doubt is attributable to some degree to the lack of space and defective ventilation of the offices occupied by our staff. I attach hereto a schedule showing the increase of work, and also a description of the rooms which we occupy. You will see that the average floor space allowed to each is only 56 square feet.
The Commissioner of Dominion Lands, Mr. Greenway reported to me that he fully endorsed this statement, and that the correspondence was bound to increase very

largely when applications for patents under the new Act would come in. In 1900 the number of files handled in the Dominion hands branch, the Assistant Commissioner's branch, was 29,263, and in 1910, 227,538. In 1900 the letters were 20,869 and in 1910 167,960.

Are these applications for
homesteads?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, they are letters with regard to homesteads. In 1900 the applications for patents were 5,601 and in 1910, 32,012. New patents recorded, 1900, 3,320; 1910, 19,352. Notifications of approval issued, in 1900, 2,746; in 1910, 19,247. The committee will thus see the enormous increase that has taken place in the past 10 years; and according to the commissioner, that increase will be much greater during the next two years, because of the very large immigration of the last two or three years, the work arising out of which has not yet reached the department.

ments of civil government, Indian Affairs, and Interior?

Does the department make any attempt whatever, to get immigrants into the eastern part of Canada. In the maritime provinces we have been suffering from loss of population, and we want immigration there just as much as in any part of Canada. I know that some time ago complaints were made, that people could not obtain any information whatever in the immigration office in London, with regard to the advantages open to settlers in the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. There was not a paper or a word of any kind about these provinces and no inducement held out to immigrants to settle there, and there are immigrants who would prefer to settle in the east, rather than in the west. I would like the hon. minister to give us some idea as to whether he has been doing anything in that respect lately, and what he has been doing.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am sorry that I am not in a position to give any details at the moment. I am only now asking for the votes for civil government and I have not the assistance here which would enable me to reply to my hon. friend's question. But I may say that we have been paying some attention to the maritime provinces during the past two or three years. We have two publications in regard to Nova Scotia, two in regard to Prince Edward Island, and one in regard to New Brunswick, publications that, I think, are fairly creditable, both to the Dominion and to the provinces concerned,-at least, I have never heard of any fault being found with them. I do not think we have any delegate now working in Great Britain from the province of New Brunswick. We have one from Nova Scotia and one from Prince Edward Island, and my information is that the results of their work have been reasonably satisfactory. Of course, the work is very different from that which is done for the rest of the Dominion. While there is the room for population in the maritime province, it is not the same kind of room as is available

in the pTairie provinces,-it is probably easier to attract immigrants to the prairie provinces than to the maritime provinces. But we realize the desirability of increasing the population of the maritime provinces in a desirable manner, and we are paying some degree of attention to it in the way I have stated. Of course, I can give my hon. friend more detailed information on another occasion.
Is it the intention of the minister to appoint one official from New Brunswick?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is our intention. We had made arrangements for the appointment, but, if my memory serves me well, the gentleman we had chosen would not accept. We have not made arrangements for a delegate from New Brunswick yet, but our desire is to have one or more delegates from each of the maritime provinces.
When some other of the minister's estimates come up, perhaps he will be in a position to give more detailed information in regard to the efforts to obtain immigration for the maritime provinces.

I understand that the province of New Brunswick have an immigration agent of their own in the old country, that province and Ontario being the only ones that have such agents. It was stated before the committee that they were working in harmony with the Dominion officials. Does the minister's department lend its assistance to these agents?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Any literature we publish is at the service of the provincial agent, and I am under the impression that the New Brunswick agent does use the literature we publish.
Do they get any other, any financial, assistance from the department?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.
Did the minister give the names of the new officials?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, we are asking for a vote which will enable us to appoint seventeen.
Have they been selected?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, we are not able to select them. We apply to the commission and they send us the candidates^ they approve of. Of course, we can reject these candidates after trial if we see fit. But, as I have said, we have found them generally satisfactory.

It is not seventeen, as I understand it; the minister is asking salaries for twenty-one new clerks. But in the
vote for contingencies there is an item ' Clerical assistance $15,000.' Last year, this was $10,000.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The amount voted for clerical assistance under contingencies is for the employment of clerks temporarily engaged during the session or in other times of rush. This is provided for under the Civil Service Act. The seventeen clerks-
Is it not twenty-one?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There are seventeen new appointments, and four promotions. Provision is made under contingencies for the appointment of extra clerks to take care of the increase of business when it is not considered desirable to make permanent increases in the staff to that extent.

As I understand these appointments, four of them are creations of new clerkships to be filled by men now in the service, leaving their present positions vacant for new appointments. It means twenty-one new appointments, and four of the clerkships are to be filled by men who are now in the service.

I assume from what the minister stated that he is in favour of the extension of the Civil Service Act. He expressed his satisfaction with the results of that Act in the inside service, and I assume that he is in favour of extending it to the outside service. May I ask what progress he has made in persuading his colleagues to adopt the provisions of the Civil Service Act in the outside service. One reason why I urge this is that there appears to be a great disparity between the salaries obtaining in the inside service and those of the outside service. I have not the figures to enable me to speak authoritatively of the salaries in the outside service, but I know from instances in my own city that they are not at all in accordance with what they are in Ottawa. In going through this list'I find there is a lot of 16 clerks who are receiving an average salary of $3,400. I question very much if that is fair; I think it is unfair relatively to the salaries obtaining particularly in the outside service in the western country. The criticism I make would apply in both ways ; first, that these salaries are too large, and secondly, that in some cases in the smaller towns they are too small. Then, going on to the next item, there are 43 clerks with an average salary of $2,500 each; next, 81 clerks with an average salary of almost $2,000'. Now, taking into consideration the very large number, it is impossible to come to the conclusion that so many high priced officials are necessary in the department. I am not criticising the staff the minister has under his control. It is

no more than justice to say, as one who has considerable to do with that staff, that I have found them exceedingly courteous and exceedingly fair. But it does appear that there is a tendency here in the city of Ottawa, in this department, and, perhaps, more so in other departments, to run the salaries beyond what would be proportionate to those obtaining throughout the length and breadth of Canada, both in the cutside service and in commercial life generally. I fancy that if the minister will look this country over, even in those parts, where living is higher than it is here, he will find that men doing the class of work that is done in his department do not receive salaries at all proportionate to these figures. It seems to me that the government has run wild, and are not considering the financial standing of the average man in Canada when they fix the salaries at such disproportionate figures. I am appealing to one of the members of the government who has had some struggles in life, perhaps, himself, the best one I can appeal to along this line, and I would ask him, first, what progress he is making in convincing his colleagues of the advisability of extending the operation of the Civil Service Act to the outside service, and, secondly, whether he does not think that, all things considered, the salaries obtaining in his department are away out of proportion, not only to those obtaining in the outside service in his own department, but to those allowed among the commercial interests of Canada to men who do the same class of work.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I regret that, as has so often happened before, it is my misfortune in life to be a disappointment to my friends. I regret to have to say that I have not exerted myself to any serious extent to secure the application of the Civil Service Act to the outside service. It has not appealed to me as likely to be a satisfactory working proposition. As to the respective salaries of the inside and outside service, I am not able from my own knowledge to make comparisons between them, or to compare them with salaries paid in other lines of life. But I would remind my hon. friend that in the Department of the Interim we are transacting the land business of, I might say, half a continent. That business is all concentrated and handled right here in Ottawa. I do not think it can be expected that business of that character and of such volume can be handled satisfactorily except by high priced men. It may be that we are paying higher salaries to some of our officials than their merits or their duties would warrant. But I will say with all candour to the committee that it is, in my poor judgment, by all odds in the best interest of Canada that where we Mr. MEIGHEN.
are handling so much and so important business we should pay salaries high enough to get men competent to handle that business. I think that is true economy and that to keep up the standard of efficiency is more important than to keep down the standard of the salaries we pay. As to salaries in the outside service, it may be that they do not compare favourably with those of the inside service in merely setting one column of figures opposite the other. I would not say that the outside service is not in many cases entitled to increase of remuneration. But there is all the difference in the world between the responsible man who is collecting the business and the man who is handling the business after it is collected. It is the difference in responsibility that is being paid for, as I understand it. I know that the salaries paid to the heads of branches here are certainly higher than the salaries paid to men on the outside, but these heads of branches have the responsibility not only for their own work, but for the work that is done by the large staff under them, and also the responsibility for the work that is done by the men in the outside service. We may be paying some of these men more than they are worth, but as an administrator of the public business I would say that the country is pursuing the line of true economy in paying sufficiently well to secure competent service.
Will the minister tell me what progress is being made towards settling the claims of applicants for homesteads in the New Westminster districts?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There are several different classes of applicants for homesteads in that district. As my hon. friend knows, the matter is one that is complicated with timber matters. He has already brought to the attention of the House one of these cases and there are others. In so far as the applications which are located within timber berths are concerned, we are not in a position to deal with them at the present time. As I have already informed my hon. friend we have had this matter under consideration for a considerable time. We find that there is a very great difference of opinion between the different interests concerned, and we have recently had representations from a deputation from one of the important interests-the lumbermen. They expressed very strong objection to the action that we had taken, and they pressed their views so strongly that we felt it was only right that we should give the matter reconsideration. Until it has become possible to give that reconsideration I cannot say how we will be able to deal with those applications.

I would like to call the minister's attention to the serious position in which he places these settlers. Their case is a very extraordinary one because nearly all of these settlers were placed on the lands by the minister's own agent at New Westminster. They went on these lands with his full knowledge and consent, and in the cases to which I refer particularly the settlers had no reason to suppose that if they fulfilled their homestead duties they would not get their patents. I have had a ream of correspondence from these settlers, and the minister has on his files a ream of correspondence setting forth the position in Which they are placed. A sample case that I will relate to him is that of George Bell-rose which was the subject of inquiry during this session. This man went on his land in 1896, speaking from recollection. The land was open for settlement. It was not part of a timber berth, but he was told when, he made his application that there was reason to suppose that correct surveys would show that an adjoining timber berth overlapped the land upon which he desired to settle. He knew that at the time but he did not know the extbnt of the overlapping which he had reason to suppose would be very small. It has now been determined that it extends over ten acres of the 160 which he attempted to take up. As to the other 150 acres there is no obstacle whatever to giving that man his patent or dealing with him in some way. The man has built a house, has brought up a family, has made an orchard, has performed all the duties that any settler could be expected to perform, he is one of the best settlers in Chilliwack, he is one of the most respectable men there, and yet in all that time he has not been able to get a title to his land. Worse than that, recently the British Columbia Electric Railway Company had occasion to cross his land. They destroyed his improvements to a large extent, they were perfectly willing to pay for the improvements as they paid all other settlers upon whose land they entered, but they found that they could not deal with Mr. Bellrose because he had no title to the land whatever. He could not be represented, as I understand it, in any negotiations respecting the amount they were to pay for the improvements that they had destroyed, but by some process they arrived at a value of $260. That value which he had created by his labour has been taken from him. The company have paid the money into the Dominion Lands office in New Westminster or elsewhere to the credit of the government. It is not the government's money, it is Mr. Bellrose's money, but he cannot get any satisfaction as to whether or not this money will be paid to him or, if it will
be paid, when it will be paid. Worse than that still, Mr. Bellrose is in this position with scores of others that if the minister's new regulations go into effect at any time before he is dealt with he will be deprived of three-quarters of his holding and, as the minister stated in this House a short time ago, under the new regulations the minister will have no power to deal with an applicant for a patent whose application has not been finally disposed of at the time the new regulations go into effect. The minister has been a pioneer himself and he can picture to himself the position in which these scores of applicants are placed through no fault of their own. It may be that the agent at New Westminster acted beyond his authority when he allowed these men to go there. I would not like to urge that upon the minister, however, because 'I know his agent at New Westminster is a very faithful servant of the department, and has spent the greater part of a lifetime in the service. I know him to be a thoroughly conscientious man, and I am quite sure that he felt that he was doing the right thing by these settlers when he placed them in the position they are now in. I am quite sure that these men were justified in relying upon verbal promises and irregular notes which they had from this agent assuring them from time to time that they were all right find that no person could turn them off their land. If the minister desires to see some of these communications I have in my possession here quite a sufficient number of them to convince him of the nature of the correspondence passing between the agent at New Westminster, and the settlers on the lands. They run something like this. The agent would write to a man who inquired why he could not get his patent :	I
cannot give you that patent because there is a new survey being made; Mr. Sound so, of the department has been up here running lines; those lines are not yet quite completed; his report has gone to Ottawa, and since it has gone there, I have not heard .anything about it; I can assure you that just as soon as I get the lines from Ottawa I will attend to your case and we will issue your patent. In several cases, he has gone further and assured the man who was anxious about his holding: You can rely upon it that no person can come between you and your claim. I have correspondence like that in this very Bellrose case, but when they write to the department they are met with an answer to which the signature of high officials of the department is attached, telling them they are mere squatters. Man after man, whose case I have brought to the attention of the department, has received a letter from the office here, that he is a mere squatter on the land, and that the department does not recognize that he

has any claim at all. I feel quite sure that the minister has no desire to leave settlers in that position. These men have committed no offence against the Dominion of Canada when they came to the province of British Columbia in answer to the minister's invitation, published in all the newspapers, to come and get land and settle upon it. They come here and they go to the office advertised, they ask the agent where they shall go, that agent puts them on a plot of land and says in the course of time, if you stay there, I will give you your patent. They have been there as long, as 15 years in the Bellrose case, and nearly as long in other cases, and these men cannot get their patents. I appeal to the Minister of the Interior that he will give some assurance that these cases will be dealt with. I am not speaking now of men settled on timber lands, where there are large quantities of timber remaining, although I think these men should have some information as to what their rights are. But, there are a number of men settled on lands not covered by timber berths and they simply have been delayed by the unravelling of the red tape of the department, and they have nothing to blame for their lack of patents, except the dilatoriness of the department based upon reasons which I cannot fathom. I would appeal to the Minister of the Interior to make some promise that whatever rights these men have, will not be jeopardized by any new regulations, and that they will remain in their present standing. That is the point of most importance to my mind, namely, to assure these men that the minister will do the square thing by them, and that if they were entitled to 160 acres under the old regulations, they will be dealt with just as effectively for them as if these old regulations had not been altered. It seems to me that is a simple thing for the minister to do, and I believe the minister has authority to do it. If the minister would only make a statement like that, it would bring comfort to a great many deserving settlers in the New Westminster district.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It would be very unwise for me to make a general statement that might be mistranslated. I wish to deal with all these settlers on a fair basis, but of course there may be a great difference of opinion as to what a fair basis is. With regard to this particular case, that my hon. friend (Mr. Taylor) mentions, I cannot understand how, if the railway company damaged Mr. Bellrose's property, the damage should be paid into the department, instead of being paid to Mr. Bellrose.
That is where it is.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
If that is where the money is now, I can assure the hon. gentleman Mr. OLIVER
that Mr. Bellrose will get it without any delay, because I think it is entirely unwarranted that the money should be paid to the department at all, it being, as my hon. friend says, Mr. Bellrose's property that was destroyed.

Subsequent to the questions recently answered by the minister about Mr. Bellrose, I sent him a copy of these answers and he acknowledged their receipt and then mentioned to me for the first time, this $260. He said: I wish you would find out if there is any prospect of my getting the $260 that the electric railway paid into the department for the damage to my property.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not see that the department has any claim on the money in any way, shape or manner, and certainly if Mr. Bellrose is entitled to it, he will get it. As to going beyond that and giving a general statement that would be assumed to be a settlement of this very complicated case, I would not like to do that, and I think my hon. friend would hardly be fair in urging it too strongly.

I ask the minister to say that these cases shall not be prejudiced by the change in the regulations, because these men have done everything in their power to have their cases settled before the regulations were changed. For instance, the present regulations were virtually suspended last July and these men have been pushing their claims actively from July to the present, which would seem to be long enough to secure settlement one way or the other, but nothing has been done.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have only apologies to offer for the fact that these matters are not settled. I do not often apologize, but I apologize in this case. There are many divergent interests to be considered and I would not wish to be tied up to a general statement, but any specific case, I would be glad to discuss. Mr. Bellrose apparently, was a squatter before the survey, and owing to the fact that part of the land he claims, is included within the timber berth, he has not so far, obtained entry for that kind, .and. therefore, is not in a position to apply for a patent. I do not know what improvements he has, but there is no doubt that whatever improvements he has, he will certainly be maintained in these improvements. There will be no question about his right to that, whatever else there may be, I myself am a pioneer and my sympathies are entirely with the pioneers, but I have to be guided in administration by all the rights and interests that are concerned, and therefore, I do not wish to go too far in making a promise.

Would it be too far for the minister to go, to say that these claims, whatever they are worth, would not be prejudiced by the changes made in the regulations, and that if these men had any rights before the regulations were changed, these rights would remain?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There has been no change t in the regulations. We proposed to make a change, but the change has not been made and I am not able to say just whether the change that we propose, will be made. So far as that is concerned, all the rights that were at any time-existing still exist without being affected in any way by the proposed regulations which were expected to go into effect last July, but which giever did go into effect.

May I go further with the minister, and ask him if he will Temove the inhibition he has placed on his agent at Westminster from dealing in any way with these applications under the old regulations, because while it is technically correct that the new regulations have not gone into effect, in another sense it is not accurate to say that, because they have been advertised as something that may go into effect at any moment, and are only temporarily suspended. As I understand it, the agent has explicit instructions not to do anything at all under the old regulations. I know that is the way he understands it- whether he has got those instructions or not-because he tells every person who goes in there, that he cannot give them any information; he cannot dot an I or cross a T or do anything that may be required to perfect any case before him. That is what these men are concerned about. If they had no rights before, they would have none now. But they see it advertised that while they have settled on 160 acres, cleared, improved and fenced it, they are likely to get patents for only 40 acres. I am sure the minister does not want to bring a man to this country on the expectation of getting 160 acres, and then pay him off with 40 acres.

If a man has settled inside a timber berth or partly inside a timber berth, I do not know how far we would be warranted in recognizing him as a legitimate squatter. If he settled entirely outside of the timber berth. I presume we would be entitled to recognize any rights he might be presumed to have; but I do not give any assurance on that point. The assurance I . am quite willing to give is that any settler outside of a timber berth, that is a man who has not trespassed on the rights of another, will get consideration for all the improvements he has made. I may say that our agent at New Westminster, although he is an old servant of the department, and I believe with the best intentions, does not perhaps fully appreciate the intricacies of the situation, and we are at present taking measures to clean up the matter and to see that people get their rights. I do not think I would be warranted in going further than that.

It seems to me that the minister might say that he would implement the promises of his agent at New Westminster, which is all that I am aiming to get. In a great many of these cases the settler has the specific assurance of the agent at New Westminster, the only man on whom the settlers can rely, and who, so far as they are concerned, is the government of Canada. They have letters from him assuring them that they will be all right. Now the minister says they will be all wrong, because his agent placed them on timber berths. The settlers did not know that he had no authority to do that; all they know is that they cannot get the papers until the timber lease is disposed of. They are quite content to wait a long time if they think they will eventually get their land; but when told that they will only get one-fourth, and that somebody else will get three-fourths of the land when divided, they feel that that is not a fair position to be placed in. It savours of repudiation of contracts which they have made with the government agent at New Westminster. The only fault that can be found with the agent is that he has been too long in the service. He has aged rapidly in late years, and is now very feeble, and the task of settling these cases is at present beyond him, because he is not physically fit to go out and make the inspections.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am quite aware that the physical infirmities of the agent have been growing upon him recently, and he is not physically able to deal with these intricate and difficult questions, and we are taking measures to have them dealt with. The clerk of the department who is in charge of that work has gone to New Westminster to try to straighten them out. As to the word of the agent binding the department, the position taken by my hon. friend is to a great extent correct; bjit where the agent has seen fit to locate a settler within a timber limit, we cannot guarantee to the settler that we will step in and take from the berth holder the right for which we have taken his money. If the agent made such a promise to any settler, he stepped outside not only of his authority, but of his right, and however willing we might be, I do not think we would be able to implement a promise of that kind to the full. All I can assure my hon. friend is that we will take into consideration the promises made by our agent to the settlers, and will implement every promise so far as it seems reasonable.
Is this $7,000 for sundries to be expended in sending some one out in behalf of these settlers?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No. That amount relates only to the travelling expenses, telegrams, postage stamps and other sundries required at the head office. It has nothing to do with the service in the west.
Contingencies, $67,000.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
This amount is made up of clerical assistance, $15,000; printing and stationery, $45,000; sundries, $7,000. The clerical assistance is required for the service of thirty temporary clerks whom it will likely be necessary to employ during the fiscal year 1911-12. These temporary clerks, in accordance with an amendment to the Civil Service Act passed last session, can be employed for a period of six months instead of four months as heretofore. We get them from the Civil Service Commission, just as we do permanent clerks. We are asking for provision for that many, but we may not require them. If not, the money will not be used. We expect, however, a very large increase in our work during the coming year.
fflimigration, $1,066,250.

I think it is the duty of the hon. minister to make a general statement such as the Minister of Railways gives us before his estimates are passed. This is a very large expenditure, and it is now too late to discuss it properly.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I would be very glad to make a general statement to-night but of course I have no desire to force the House to go on.
If my hon. friend would fix a day for the discussion, that would be a considerable convenience.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Unless something unfor-seen should occur, we will say Friday next.
Some resolutions reported.
Mr. FIELDING moved the adjournment of the House.

The leader of the opposition has requested me to give the following notice on his behalf: As the pending reciprocity proposals have not been carried into effect by the Congress of the United States at the session which has just terminated, he intends to move on Wednesday next for the postponement of the further consideration of these proposals in the parliament of Canada.
Motion agreed to, and the House adjourned at 11.23 p.m.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Tuesday, March 7, 1911.
